Mr. Speaker, the whole purpose of the conference was to reverse the trend of the past two years during which Canada was not competitive in its price and cost structure. The premiers and I agreed that in order to achieve that purpose we had to do several things. One of them was to bring down inflation, the CPI, to a rate of 3*/2 per cent within the next three years. The second was to keep down the cost of government growth. The third was to create confidence in the private sector so that the private sector would, with renewed confidence in the economy, create the jobs which are needed. The fourth was to specify a certain number of projects which the governments together could get under way now or in the short term.

mined to make these optimistic projections a reality. They know they will do it if they can instil into the private sector, by which I mean the unions and management, the same kind of confidence that we in the governments of this country feel.

Is the Prime Minister not prepared to cut taxes for medium and low income taxpayers? Is he not prepared to expand the housing budget? I point out that the government made no specific short-run proposals, nor did it set up specific means of achieving its main targets.

If the leader of the NDP is referring to some suggestions made at St. Andrews by the premiers, I would point out to him that the same premiers, with one change, were present at the conference during the last few days. All this led the premiers and myself to the conclusion that the economy would not perform in the years to come as it has in the past two years, because steps have been taken and policy decisions have been taken and implemented which will produce better results. This is extremely important in the eyes of all who took part in the conference.

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-REMARKS ATTRIBUTED TO SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege concerns remarks attributed to the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) today by the news media, a great part of which refers to me. The minister is reported to have said that RCMP security officials approached me for evidence with regard to the matter I raised in this House on June 1, 1977, namely, the training of persons in terrorist activities under the auspices of the Russian KGB at a training camp located at Finsterwalde, East Germany.
The following appears in the media: Asked whether the government is trying to find out who my informants are, the minister is reported to have stated that when security officers of the RCMP approached me, "nothing was forthcoming".
February 16, 1978

The minister has made an entirely misleading and inaccurate statement which I suggest casts reflections on me as a member of parliament and constitutes a matter of privilege.
The facts are these: I was approached shortly after I raised the matter of Finsterwalde in the Flouse by two members of the security service of the RCMP and, if I remember correctly, their names were Inspector Don MacKinnon and Corporal Dwight Dowbiggin. They asked me if I would give them the name and address of the source of my information. I assured them that I was prepared to co-operate to the fullest extent, but I added that I could furnish the name only if the individual was in agreement. I explained to the RCMP on the day in question that the individual was in Europe travelling behind the so-called iron curtain. I further explained that his ability to travel behind the iron curtain could be severely hampered and, indeed, that his life could be endangered if there happened to be a double-agent within the RCMP who came across the name and passed it on to Soviet sources.
The officers fully agreed, but attempted to obtain the name on the basis of assurances that there was really no possibility of there ever being a double-agent within the RCMP and that, due to recruitment methods followed by the security service, this was in practice impossible. Needless to say, the incident revealed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) a few days ago regarding the expulsion of 13 Soviet diplomats because of attempts to infiltrate the security service of the RCMP, and their belief that they had actually done so, indicates clearly that I had every right to be concerned. It was not a matter of my not co-operating. The situation in England a few years ago in which Kim Philby, head of British counter intelligence, turned out to be a Soviet agent is a further example which speaks for itself.
In effect the Solicitor General has accused me of not co-operating with the RCMP. On the contrary, I eventually contacted my source when it was possible and was refused permission to divulge his identity to the police, and I advised them accordingly.
The Solicitor General is quoted further as saying that we are in "a very ticklish situation at a very ticklish time". While I agree with that, I cannot agree with something else the minister is quoted as saying, which I think constitutes another matter of privilege.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-REMARKS ATTRIBUTED TO SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Order, please. I hope the hon. member understands that one of the difficulties I have is deciphering what part of his argument is with respect to disagreement with the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) and what part, if any, constitutes privilege. The hon. member is now going on to cite another matter about which he just said he disagrees with the Solicitor General. Matters about which there is disagreement between the hon. member and the Solicitor General are not matters of privilege, as the hon. member understands, and I would like to be sure that he confines himself strictly to matters which might relate to privilege.

subsubtopic: MR. COSSITT-REMARKS ATTRIBUTED TO SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
I agree, Mr. Speaker. I used the wrong phrase. There is no question about that.
Business of the House
The Solicitor General was quoted further as saying that he was prepared to make information available to members of parliament later in the spring on matters I have raised, but only if they swear to keep details secret. Fie is reported to have added that some of the information would be given to members of parliament only under oath, but not all of it. This indicates to me an attempt by the Solicitor General to suppress the privileges of members of parliament, who are elected by the Canadian people to run this country, as if they cannot be trusted without having to take special oaths, and the implication is that with respect to some information the government would not trust members of parliament anyway, even under oath.
Finally, I submit that the Solicitor General has done the following things which breach my privileges and the privileges of others in this House: He has falsely stated and implied that I did not co-operate with the RCMP security service, and he has certainly implied that members of parliament are not to be trusted.
I feel justified in demanding that the Solicitor General withdraw his uncalled for remarks with regard to me and other members of this House. This parliament should not tolerate inaccurate and untruthful statements by the man in charge of law enforcement in Canada, who has demonstrated clearly his utter and total incompetence.
I reserve my right to move any motion which might become necessary arising from this matter.

subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX ON PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
1.	Is the government giving any consideration to replacing the ten cent per gallon excise tax on gasoline used for private purposes with a three cent per gallon excise tax on all petroleum products as recommended by the Canadian Automobile Association and (a) if so, on what date will the change be made (b) if not, for what reason?
2.	Has the government undertaken any studies to determine the effectiveness of the excise tax on gasoline in promoting energy conservation and (a) if so, what were the results (b) if not, for what reason?
3.	Is the government giving any consideration to requiring motor vehicle manufacturers and their agents to indicate on any bill of sale all federal and provincial taxes and thereby inform consumers where their money is going?
4.	(a) Has the government undertaken any studies to evaluate the effectiveness of the weight and air conditioner tax, imposed on automobiles as an energy conservation measure and (i) if so, what were the results (ii) if not, for what reason (b) if this tax is found ineffective, will the government consider removing it and if it is found effective, will the government require it to be clearly stated as additional taxes on any bill of sale?

speakeroldname: Mr. Yvon Pinard (Parliamentary Secretary to President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: EXCISE TAX ON PETROLEUM PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Finance and Energy, Mines and Resources as follows: 1. The government is continuously reviewing and evaluating proposed legislative changes. With regard to the proposal for replacing the ten cent per gallon excise tax on gasoline for personal use with a three cent per gallon tax on all petroleum products, it is considered that such a change is not a viable alternative at this time. The increase in the price of crude oil is affecting the prices of all petroleum products. The existing excise tax on motor gasoline for personal use provides a further incentive to conservation in an area of petroleum use where it appears easier for consumers to make additional adjustments in consumption patterns. Imposition of a tax on all users would unduly raise the cost of home heating and have adverse effects on Canada's competitive position by raising producers' costs.
2. No. (a) Not applicable, (b) The excise tax was not designed primarily as an energy conservation measure. The ten cent per gallon excise tax on gasoline for personal use is one of a number of influences on the demand for gasoline. These include the increase in the price of crude oil, the mileage requirements for automobiles set by EMR, the excise tax on heavy cars and other excise taxes on energy consuming products. It is difficult to disentangle the effects of all relevant influences on sales of motor gasoline so as to determine the
precise importance of the excise tax in terms of energy conservation. It should be noted, however, that there is broad agreement among researchers that consumer demand for motor gasoline is responsive to changes in the price of the product.
3.	No mechanism exists whereby retailers can be forced to display federal taxes on their bills of sale to consumers. Federal commodity taxes are imposed at the manufacturer's level and as such become an element in the retailer's cost. This is not unlike other taxes or costs incurred by the retailer, such as realty taxes, tax on corporate profit, the employee's share of Canada pension, unemployment insurance, workmen's compensation, hospitalization etc., which are passed on to the consumer but are not identified on the bill of sale. With regard to provincial taxes, this matter is the responsibility of the individual provinces concerned and as such is outside the area of federal jurisdiction.
4.	(a) The weight tax on heavy automobiles is just one of a number of government measures and market circumstances that bear on consumer and producer choices as to the relative desirability of buying and producing various types of automobiles. For example, the mileage requirements set by EMR and the increase in the price of motor gasoline resulting from both higher crude oil prices and the ten cent per gallon excise tax, make heavier, less fuel-efficient automobiles less desirable. While it is difficult to isolate the precise effects of each individual measure, it is clear that the tendency is toward the use of smaller, lighter, more fuel-efficient vehicles. The $100 excise tax on air conditioners represents a significant deterrent to their purchase. Comparisons of revenue collected and sales of vehicles over recent months with data for the 1975 calendar year (the latest for which actual data on air conditioners sales exist), indicate a significant increase in the percentages of new cars not equipped with air conditioners. While this could be in response to several influences which are difficult to isolate, it is thought that the tax is a significant factor, (b) The question of the identification of federal taxes as a separate item on the retailer's bill of sale was addressed in question 3.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before presenting my case for the resolution, I should like to clear away a little piece of debris which also helps to point up one of the things that has been wrong with the general approach in the fight against regional disparities in the area being considered by the House today.
Yesterday in reply to a question, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) gave the impression that somehow a royal commission appointed by the government led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) imposed upon the minority Pearson government the necessity to pass legislation governing freight rates which the Minister of Transport does not approve of today. The minister correctly pointed out that this legislation provided inadequate regulation of freight rates in areas where competition was limited. The minister tried to give the impression that this was somehow or other imposed upon a minority government. He said, for example, that the reason freight rates are what they are is that after the MacPherson commission set up by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, the minority parliament enacted legislation which gave, essentially, freedom to the railways to set rates on the principle of what the market would bear, on the theory that competition would control the situation.
In my opinion this has worked to the detriment of the Atlantic area. I happened to be premier of Nova Scotia at the time this legislation was being drafted and considered by the government and put through the House. All Atlantic governments opposed it on the grounds the minister mentioned yesterday. The Maritime Transportation Commission opposed it, yet the government insisted on passing the legislation in the form it was adopted.
For the minister to suggest that the Liberal government of the day was somehow pressed into adopting the legislation by a royal commission is to suggest that the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, who was Minister of Transport at the time, was a patsy- which he was not, whatever else he was-and that he completely falsified history.
It is the kind of distortion and political falsification which we do not need, particularly in the case of regional disparity and its causes. This is the kind of distortion and falsification

February 16, 1978
Regional Disparities
that increased my own personal doubts about how much one can believe of many of the statements being made by ministers these days.
I deliberately made that statement at the beginning, Mr. Speaker, because it is not my intention to generate any partisan heat in the course of this debate.
I wish to focus attention on a serious and deepening national problem and the urgency in facing it. As I indicated, the way in which freight rate legislation and the control of freight rates have worked against regional economic development in the Atlantic area is an example of what I have in mind.
First of all, there is much about regional economic disparity we can agree on; it exists as far a- the Atlantic provinces are concerned. It is serious, and it is clear the approaches in dealing with it are inadequate. Ten years ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a commitment at a time when he had not given it much thought. The problem was how to attack regional economic disparity. Fie promised the establishment of a department, which became DREE. At that time I expressed some reservations concerning the ability of such a department to co-ordinate adequately the operation of the federal government. I expressed some reservations about the whole approach and I think they were justified. In any event, whether they were justified or not, surely the time has come for a thorough review of the policy and approaches that have been followed during the last decade. I want to do this without threshing over too much old straw and I do not propose to spend much time on statistics.
There is clearly serious unemployment in eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. There is a serious gap in the per capita income in that area as compared with the rest of the country. This gap exists despite very substantial transfer payments. Indeed, in a very real sense the economic weakness of that region is more serious than the income disparity would indicate because transfer payments have, in fact, shored up, and continue to shore up the income figures.
The economy of that region is relatively weaker vis-a-vis the rest of Canada than it was ten years ago. And I say that very deliberately, Mr. Speaker. I do not say this to spread gloom or doom, or anything like that. It is not that there are no opportunities in that region, there are opportunities. There are opportunities in industries such as fisheries, by way of tidal power development and power development generally, and many things that no doubt DREE has under consideration.
It is not a matter of being gloomy, it is a matter of recognizing that far from making progress the economy has slipped in terms of strength relative to the rest of the country. This to some extent has been disguised by the increase in transfer payments from the Government of Canada to those areas. It is time for a thorough review of policies.
I do not think DREE has ever been in the position to develop and implement a coherent strategy to attack economic policies in that area. There have been attacks launched against particular problems. There have been agreements entered into

concerning problems in sections of the Atlantic provinces. There have been useful steps taken to help develop the infrastructure in various parts of the Atlantic provinces. I, for one, have never been able to see what seems to me to be essential, a plan or a strategy involving the co-ordinated efforts of all the federal departments and agencies. This should be a plan not imposed on the Atlantic provinces, but worked out with their governments, and followed by their governments, a coherent, co-ordinated and co-operative effort. Whatever else is essential to attack problems of regional disparity in that area, those requirements are essential and we have not met them, Mr. Speaker.
Some are questioning not only the lack of coherency, the lack of co-operation and the lack of co-ordination, but also whether what has been done is moving things in the right direction at all.
In a recent lecture, which was described as deliberately provocative, Professor Thomas H. Courchene of the University of London, has argued that the effect of transfer and other policies in recent years has been to worsen the economies of the poorer provinces. In the introduction to his lecture he says that the current system of transfers, between governments and from governments to persons, is not at all conducive to eliminating regional economic differentials in this country.
Indeed I should argue the current pattern of transfers is serving to rigidify, perhaps even exacerbate provincial and regional disparities. 1 do not think one has to accept all of that to recognize that there may be some questions to be asked, or to agree fairly substantially with what Professor Courchene declares on page 17 of these lectures, when he says that "The thrust of the above analysis suggests that the economies of the have-not provinces are likely to have deteriorated relatively over time" which is my own view-"deteriorated in a sense they are put in a position where to an increasing extent they rely on federal transfers for their well being."
Put more bluntly, the result of the combined policies with respect to Canada's various regions is such that to a substantial degree Canada has turned several provincial economies into what financial analyst Don McGillivray has referred to as government dependencies. As a native Nova Scotian 1 do not read that with any great pleasure. It seems to me there is some element of truth and that we have and are creating governmental dependencies. I do not suggest the federal government is solely to blame for this. I believe that George Post, at the time acting chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, hit the nail pretty well on the head when he said to the Chronicle-Herald on September 20, 1977:
It's never quite the right time for governments to engage in bold new initiatives, ... Some day, governments are going to have to face the disparity issue,... The problem shows not the slightest indication of going away on its own.
I think, Mr. Speaker, the time has come to take a clear, hard look at what has been going on. Some bold new initiatives and approaches should be conceived and implemented. It is not simply a matter of me expressing opinions or academics like Professor Courchene. A senior Newfoundland minister recent-
February 16, 1978

ly declared that the effort to achieve economic development, as contrasted to what has been done to improve infrastructure, had been a failure.
Surely in view of these statements, and in view of what we can all see, it is necessary to take a hard look at what that minister described as a failure, and try to do something better. As I say, and I cannot repeat it too often, a basic condition for doing better is a thorough co-ordination of federal effort and the thorough co-operation of the concerned provinces with the federal government in attacking the problems of the region.
It may be that the problems and opportunities in Newfoundland, Labrador, and eastern Quebec are sufficiently different from those of the maritime provinces to require, in part at least, a distinctive approach from what would be appropriate for the maritime provinces. However, the federal and provincial governments, and I deliberately say federal and provincial, must have enough political courage to take a regional approach. This would not please every provincial or federal constituency in the region. Any coherent and effective plan to attack the causes of regional disparity may seem unfair for the time being to some sections in that region. The governments must have the intestinal fortitude to face that complaint. They must not be frightened by complaints that another province or another section in their own province is doing better and, as a result, the regional effort is disrupted. No approach will be absolutely fair to all at the same time. Lord knows there is plenty of intraregional disparity now, plenty of economic disparity within the region. It may indeed be as great as the disparity between the region and the rest of the country.
In terms of getting agreement, understanding, approval of an approach within the area, and of getting the people in various walks of life and different sectors of the economy behind a program, the people should be more involved in developing it. I am not suggesting that the ministers of this government should be following absolutely a program such as the one we had in Nova Scotia, called Voluntary Economic Planning. It involved representatives of business, labour, farmers and other people in developing a planned approach. It was not simply a matter of people accepting something produced by the bureaucrats and the politicians, but rather of developing an approach together.
If this is a practical way to proceed in the maritime provinces, it could diminish enormously the distrust between different provinces, the distrust between different sections of the provinces, and could increase enormously the support that any strategy or approach would receive from the total area. It is worth thinking about some variation of that kind of approach, plan, or method of policy. I believe it is worth considering the application of this to the maritimes as a whole.
When I talk about maritime co-operation I want to make it very clear that I am not proposing, at this time at least, maritime governmental union. I want that made clear. It has been recommended by a commission, but it has not yet been
Regional Disparities
adopted and I see no sign of it being adopted. I do not wish to drag any red herrings around at this time.
There has been a degree of co-operation developed among the maritime provinces. However, one sometimes gets the impression that competition is being stressed more than cooperation. When the going gets tough, competition between the provinces takes over. It may not be a big matter, but there has been feuding over the location of the veterinary college. Anybody who has been following the situation can mention other instances where one province is seen to have difficulty going along with the others.
Co-operation between or among the provinces cannot be just a matter of convenience. It must be a governing factor at all times. Newfoundland-Labrador and eastern Quebec may be sufficiently distinct, but surely it makes sense from a national point of view to treat the maritimes as a unit of economic development. That does not mean the federal government should impose on those three provinces a plan of development. It does mean that the federal government should insist on a common plan of development and a common strategy to be developed by the people of the three provinces and the federal government. Once that plan or strategy has been agreed upon by everyone concerned, the federal government, its departments and agencies and the provinces, that strategy or plan could only be changed by agreement.
The federal government must show leadership here. That is not to say the total responsibility rests with the Government of Canada. I do not believe that. However, it must take the leadership. The governments and the people of the region must have their responsibility as well. Let us have an end to ad hoc federal initiatives and an end to ad hoc demands for federal action on particular problems. They have never amounted to an adequate approach and they certainly do not now. In fact, they are creating a complex of dependence.
I do not suggest that all decisions on projects be postponed until there is agreement on a strategy or plan. Far from it. There are measures in particular sectors that should go forward promptly, ones that would clearly be right and appropriate under any plan. Some of these will be suggested today by colleagues who will follow me in speaking, in the areas of fisheries, development and transportation. These specific measures will be full of merit. Many meritorious suggestions have come forth from the maritime provinces. These specific measures in particular sectors will not be enough in themselves to constitute a coherent and adequate plan to lift the economy of the maritimes and the Atlantic provinces as we want to see done.
The governments must do some pretty fundamental thinking about the total strategy. I am not suggesting one should accept all the doubts created by Professor Courchene and other academics, thoughtful men no doubt. Nevertheless, after ten years of government under the present Prime Minister, eight years of DREE, and after what any fair minded person must qualify at best a very limited success, it is surely time to take a very searching look at what has been going on, what has worked, what has not worked, and what is the trouble.
2926

February 16, 1978
Regional Disparities
Because of my strong belief about the need for review, I am happy to see the academics looking at this. I was pleased to see the Economic Council of Canada study regional disparity. It published the findings of its study in a report called "Living Together".
This is not the first time the Economic Council of Canada has taken a very comprehensive and helpful look at this problem. When Mr. Deutsch was chairman of the council in the sixties, the council published a very comprehensive study of the problems of regional disparity in Canada. It is my hope that the new chairman of the Economic Council will keep this great national problem very high on her list of priorities for the council to study.
There seems to be, as I will indicate in a few moments, a substantial difference of opinion between the Economic Council and the Department of Finance, to mention one department. For all I know, there may be a substantial difference of opinion between the council and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. It is essential that they all get together to do their thinking and try to come together in their assessment of what needs to be done.
At the time of this report last year, the acting chairman described governmental response to it as "underwhelming". That is the word he used to describe the reaction in government circles. The Economic Council highlighted one factor in its report. It noted that unemployment increases more rapidly in the Atlantic provinces than in other provinces during a national economic recession. Simply put, the report suggested that this means that effective demand falls more in the Atlantic provinces than elsewhere as a result of a national recession. The report made some recommendations. It recommended a joint federal-provincial effort to offset this factor through a fiscal stabilization plan, part of which might involve temporary tax cuts, directed to the Atlantic provinces and not to the rest of Canada.
This is not the only point made by the council in this report, but I was interested to find the council pushing hard the view that during a recession the economy of the Atlantic provinces falls further behind than is the case with respect to the economies in other parts of the country. Whatever one thinks about the solution the Economic Council proposed, its analysis of the problem is very impressive.
We in the maritimes have always felt in our gut that economic depressions or recessions slowed down our growth more than was the case in the rest of Canada; that we were usually the first to be hit and the last to recover, and that any momentum we got going during the upward movement of the economy was destroyed during the recession and became very difficult to restore. If this gut feeling is right, if the analysis made by the Economic Council is right, this explains a good deal of the chronic weakness in the economies of the areas to which I have referred. If national recessions-and they come every few years-have a much greater impact upon the Atlan-

tic region than upon the rest of the country, then the effect becomes cumulative.
After reading this report, I wrote to the minister of finance of that day, now the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald), asking what the Department of Finance thought about this point made by the Economic Council and about its proposals to correct the situation. The minister was most responsive and I want to thank him publicly now for his courtesy in replying at length. He wrote me a long letter setting forth the department's reaction.
The department did not accept the council's contention that, because unemployment rises faster in the Atlantic provinces during a national recession, the economies of those provinces are necessarily set back further than they are in the other provinces. It stated that unemployment swings down further during recovery than it does in other provinces-not to a lower point, of course-and that consequently the entire cycle does not hurt the Atlantic economy. The department argued that during national recovery the drop in the rate of unemployment was greater in the Atlantic provinces than in the country at large. The former minister argued, also, that although unemployment rises to a higher point in the eastern provinces during a recession, output does not.
I must say I do not find the department's response to the analysis of the Economic Council very convincing. This may not indicate that the department is wrong, but I find myself still siding with the Economic Council. To my mind it does not explain away the effect of recession on the Atlantic economy. As to the council's proposals to stimulate effective demand and employment by a policy of fiscal stabilization, the department pretty well dismisses it out of hand, on the whole, I thought, with arguments which are reasonably convincing. I am not prepared to make a case for the remedial measures the council proposed.
Toward the conclusion of his letter the former minister wrote:
It is far from clear that the new approaches proposed by the council offer any net advantage over the approaches already being used in the effort to lessen regional disparities. It may be noted that a number of approaches already in use, including DREE grants and the regionally differentiated investment tax creadit of the last budget involve specific incentives to locate economic activity in the target areas. In general, this seems to us likely to be more effective than less direct approaches.
As I have indicated, I accept his criticism of the solutions proposed by the Economic Council but I have to say that while the hon. member for Rosedale was persuaded that the methods being employed were probably more effective than those proposed by the Economic Council, those methods have not yet shown anything which could be considered hopeful by way of results. I believe the Economic Council drew attention to a very serious problem and that its analysis was significant.

speechtext:
I apologize to the House, Mr. Speaker. I will wind up very shortly. To sum up, we have to examine what has been going on in other departments. We have to insist upon co-operation and co-ordination. We have to pay strict attention to the analysis of the problem put out by the Economic Council. And we must pay attention to something else which was said by the hon. member for Rosedale while he was minister of finance.
The very fact that such a substantial government effort had to be made in order to achieve results would seem to indicate that there are limits to what the government can accomplish when it moves to counter the economic forces producing regional disparities. I am not saying we could not perhaps do more in this regard, but that we should not expect government policies to completely eliminate regional disparities. For this to occur, the proper conditions must exist in the private sector of the economy.
What does that mean? I thought this was what we were trying to create. I thought we were trying to create proper conditions in the private sector in eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. Was the minister suggesting there is something wrong with attitudes or with the organization of industry in that region of Canada? Was he suggesting there are marketing difficulties? What, in the view of the Department of Finance or of the government generally, are the proper conditions? What are the weaknesses which exist today? I think it is time for frankness. I do not expect the government to commit hara-kiri by saying things which are offensive to the people of that region, but if there is something wrong with existing conditions such as to prevent enterprise from developing in the region, I think it should be discussed.
Of course the classic grievance in the eastern provinces arises from the very shape of the Canadian market which at the present time offers such striking advantages to industry in central Canada. I think we ought to be considering ways of overcoming this situation which has been a significant cause of regional disparity. Unless we can do something to change the shape of the market, the areas we are talking about today will increasingly become colonial economic dependencies of central Canada.
What are the weaknesses in the private sector? Granted, the government cannot do everything itself. My colleagues will be putting forward specific proposals.
In summary, my case is very simple. We have not been successful. By "we" I mean the Government of Canada; the Parliament of Canada; the government, the legislatures, and the people of the areas concerned. We have had very limited success, to the degree we have had any success at all, in confronting these problems over the last decade.
In order to have success we must have a coherent, co-operative, co-ordinated policy. Personally I am not happy. Huge sums are being spent, and the economy is not strengthening. I am not happy when I see the governments in the area I come from becoming increasingly dependent on the federal government, nor the increasing discouragement which I sense there. Not just the federal government, the provincial governments, and the people of the region, but everyone should accept their
Regional Disparities
responsibilities and face reality. The beginning of this process is a review of what is going on. Certainly it includes the whole-hearted co-operation of provincial governments. It requires leadership from the Government of Canada, and that is what I ask for today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words are of course directed to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) whose sense of moderation and responsibility in debating such serious issues I always admire. He almost always shows that attitude anyway, I think, and I believe he considers the economic problems prevailing in the Atlantic provinces and in Quebec as a very serious issue.
I wish to congratulate and thank him for having given us the opportunity to discuss regional disparities, the particular economic situation of eastern Quebec the Atlantic provinces, as well as the efforts that have been made, the successes achieved and, above all, the important challenge facing us. I thank him for the opportunity he has given us, Mr. Speaker, and I want the House to know that during the time allotted to me I will try to talk the way he has, that is in a general way at the beginning, but also in a rather selective way as regards what we have done in the past, what we are doing now and what we hope to be able to achieve with the co-operation of the provinces in the coming months and years.

I welcome the opportunity to speak to this motion, particularly in light of the discussion related to regional policies and regional development which took place at the conference of first ministers. As hon. members know, I participated in a number of the sectoral conferences leading up to the conference of first ministers and was represented by senior officials on the federal delegation to others. The DREE input to these conferences was significant and the DREE presence was widely appreciated, indicating as it did the emphasis which the federal government has been giving, increasingly in recent years, to the regional dimension of policies affecting economic

development. This dimension received a good deal of attention at the meeting of finance ministers and at the conference of first ministers itself, where it was represented by a separate item on the agenda. The lead speaker for that item was Premier Hatfield of New Brunswick. I should like to refer to some of the comments he made concerning that particular topic. Page 5 of his statement reads as follows:
Looking beyond the cyclical condition, I think that very significant progress has been made in broadening the economic base in many of the poorer regions. It is this longer term improvement which should permit us to make significant gains once the economy returns to more normal levels.
Let me try to illustrate this for the Atlantic provinces.
One key indicator of the basis for growth in the Atlantic region is the amount of fixed capital stock. There has been an impressive growth in the real level of capital stock. For instance, between 1961 and 1974, total fixed capital in the Atlantic provinces increased at an average annual rate of 9 per cent-almost two percentage points higher than the rate of growth in Ontario.
Before the cyclical downturn, when capacity utilization declined across the country, this investment was reflected in impressive growth in output and employment. For example, from 1966 to 1974, the value of Atlantic manufacturing output grew at an average annual rate of 24 per cent-a full nine points above the national average. Over the same period, Atlantic manufacturing employment increased at an average rate of nearly 2 per cent-almost twice the Canadian average.
Witf respect to the need for modification to the approach of DREE, he said:
Both the investment tax credit and the recently announced employment tax credit have been designed to provide additional assistance in the DREE designated areas.
He referred to other tools, other means, and other departments becoming involved in fighting disparities. He said:
Programs of the federal government must continue to be increasingly designed with regional development needs in mind. The most important method in achieving a co-ordinated approach to regional development at the present time, however, is that of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
Also he said:
We should give DREE a good deal of credit for what it has achieved and we cannot blame regional development policies for the setbacks resulting from cyclical difficulties.

Mr. Speaker, those were the comments of premier Hatfield which, were taken up again by several other Canadian premiers with slight differences of course. I would like to take this opportunity to deal with part of the motion now under consideration in which the hon. member for Halifax is asking the government to renew its commitment to reduce regional disparities. I would like once again to quote from the press release at the end of the conference which is rather explicit on regional disparities, and I quote:
First ministers strongly affirmed the importance of reducing regional disparities and the continuing need for review and expansion of programs for regional development, based on the longer-run economic development potential and transportation requirements of each province and region.
It was also agreed that we should continue to be the major federal agency for these purposes. So definitely we have a commitment here by both levels of government to carry on our joint efforts in reducing regional disoarities.


Mr. Speaker, I am going to spend a few moments dealing with the Atlantic region which presents enough reasons to concern my department. There are enough on going projects to say a few words about them. When this department was established, we have worked in terms of designated and specially designated areas. It was an approach which at the time was in the line of thoughts of the hon. member for Halifax who recognized the potential and the existence of some centers and poles of growth. Both levels of governments identified some poles of growth and established a program of expansion to create in those places a situation which would stimulate the expansion of businesses. We have witnessed the establishment of such centres in each one of the maritime provinces as well as in Quebec, in the prairie provinces, in Ontario and even in British Columbia.
As the hon. member has pointed out, after a few years this approach has proved to be valuable but it also had weaknesses, as a result of which the efforts of the federal and provincial governments were concentrated in very specific areas within the provinces. The hon. member-and I commend him for his position-has recognized that it was always hard to be selective in that kind of action, that while we recognized the growth potential of some regions, we denied such recognition to other areas of those same provinces.
After spending tens of millions of dollars in these expansion centers over a period of three or four years, we finally realized that by doing so-something the Economic Council of Canada has recognized for that matter-we had in fact contributed to widening the income gap between expansion center residents and people in other areas of these provinces. This had become evident, for instance, in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and indeed in Newfoundland: in St. John's where our expansion center was located, the incomes of the local residents increased much more rapidly than elsewhere in the province, therefore we would constantly receive a great many representations for the implementation of similar programs within these regions and sub-regions. While continuing to provide assistance to the expansion centers which we had identified, we had the opportunity, through the General Development Agreements and subagreements we had with the provinces, to open new areas for development ir. these subregions.
When the hon. member suggests that we should take a more comprehensive approach and have a master plan for all the Maritimes excluding Newfoundland to which he recognizes a somewhat different status, I fully agree with him in principle. One wonders how it would be done while respecting, of course, the provinces' will and authority as well as the potential and the projects that may be carried out. We thought it could be done by stages. The GDA entered into with each one of the provinces is one step which brings us closer, of course to a consensus among the Atlantic authorities on the need for shared costs programs.
The Council of Maritimes Premiers is helped financially by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The department also supports many projects which are jointly decided
February 16, 1978

upon by the three Atlantic premiers. I believe it is a good start in the right direction. The hon. member has pointed out some difficulties. There has been agreement on some projects we have carried out together, but then there was some disagreement. It is not easy, and the hon. member quite agreed.
Now, to come back to that new framework, known as the general development agreement and subagreements, 1 feel that we have there a new approach for planning, analysing, identifying and coordinating our work which is by far superior to what we had before. It may not be perfect, as I am the first to admit but it will provide us with an opportunity for better co-ordination between both federal levels of government and later on, various departments.
When I took this portfolio over two years ago, we had just a few subagreements in operation. The House may be interested to know that since the model agreement for development has been signed, we have negotiated and signed, with the provinces of Canada, 78 agreements which were amended in 80 instances. Thus, we have been practically negotiating new agreements all the time or amending existing ones. That process may seem cumbersome and slow, but it is one of joint assessment studies.
It is a planning process, one through which the efforts of several federal departments are co-ordinated with a view to maximizing the impact of federal interventions in various regions through the subagreements I have mentioned. As recently as last week, I signed an agreement with the province of Alberta; we travelled up north in that province, to Fort Vermilion, close to the 60th parallel, and met with officials of that community which, for practical purposes is in a sense the capital of the area where the agreement will be implemented. Two of my colleagues joined me in signing that agreement. And together with the government of Alberta we will be able to deal with problems in the northern part of that province, problems affecting small groups of people, whether they are natives of the area, Indians, Metis or white people. This is a co-ordinated effort. But in three Atlantic provinces as a whole-because Prince Edward Island must always be excluded as it has a very special agreement-we now have 38 agreements that have been signed and already amended 55 times for very substantial amounts touching practically every sector of the economy.
In his last remarks the hon. member asked why, when there is an economic recession, the Atlantic provinces and eastern Quebec-a good part of Quebec-are always more rapidly and severely affected, and when an upturn occurs only after central Canada has regained strength do the Atlantic regions and Quebec start feeling the beneficial effects. This is a matter that other levels of government neglected and with which we are concerned.
What conditions could be achieved in those provinces so that when we have a recession it would affect the Atlantic region less or at least no more than the other parts of this country? I do not think that any of them are being treated more favour-
Regional Disparities
ably than the others. But what we would like to try and do is find out how we could develop the economic industrial structure in the Atlantic provinces, as the hon. member pointed out, so that when there are hard times in the international context the same area will not always be the one to be affected.
It is difficult to give an answer to that. We think that by improving various forms of infrastructures-and when my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) referred earlier to the statement he made, of course the first years were not a success from an industrial standpoint. A few gains were recorded. In the case of his province, Newfoundland, our greatest efforts were designed to develop the infrastructure and help the province to manage more efficiently its resources: forestry, the mining sector, energy and particularly hydroelectricity, through existing agreements, and there is quite an impressive list of 13 agreements that have been amended 34 times in the case of Newfoundland, as we want that flexibility to adapt our programs to the opportunities identified by the province itself. We want the province of Newfoundland to develop its potential, and this is also true of every province.
It was recognized that if the economy of Newfoundland was to be strengthened so as to be able to weather bad times, its base should be reinforced. In fact, it had a poor highway system and in many places an inadequate school system, and in some municipalities there was no infrastructure at all,
I think we had many reasons to take some action designed to reinforce the position of those provinces. The economic deterioration of the Atlantic provinces is a trend that developed over a period of at least 50 years or even 100 years. It is obvious that we shall have to develop a long-term strategy to remedy the situation. It will require a sustained and significant effort. And then, of course, we may not agree on the level of funding and financial commitment by the federal government to help Atlantic provinces develop their economies and over come their economic short comings.
I will not deal in depth with the case of Prince Edward Island as my colleague, the hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) will have an opportunity to raise that issue and I assume that as a representative of Prince Edward Island, he will be willing to speak about his own province. I will therefore limit my remarks to the three other provinces.
A study of the programs now in place in those three other provinces, namely Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, shows that we are now working to develop their forest resources. We have set up procedures to carry out inventories, analyses and careful identification of these resources, and to build access roads and carry out a reforestation program.
Finally, we have helped establish what has been commonly referred to as forest resources management in those three provinces. It did not exist previously or at least if it did, it was very fragmentary. This is an extremely important resource for those provinces and I think we had to tackle these problems and try to develop their potentials.

In other provinces, more particularly in New Brunswick and Newfoundland, we noted that the road ways were run down. In Nova Scotia we conducted three or four major studies on that issue. We found that the situation in Newfoundland is particularly serious. Over the past five years in particular, we kept pouring money in to improve the road infrastructures in that province and provide means for the development and transportation of those resources. This required large amounts of money.
Mr. Speaker, I could mention several other areas. Tourism is a resource that we are now developing after identifying several sectors. In the province of New Brunswick, for instance, 15 existing agreements have been amended 28 times. This shows the flexibility of our approach. We want to be able to plan with the province. Our aim, perhaps on the rather long term, is to achieve a comprehensive planning and recognize the specific nature and advantages of each province.
It is very important to capitalize on the real advantages that exist in these provinces since it may be dangerous to establish industries there which have no affinity with the area. We have tried this approach and it has failed. We have had certain failures, but we have also had some success. There is, for instance, the case of the Michelin company in Nova Scotia. This is an obvious example of a major intervention on the part of the government which has been and still is completely successful. However, there have been other interventions which were not as successful, and we recognize this.
We have the honesty to admit making mistakes occasionally, we recognize that situations have changed. We are not the only ones to have made mistakes, the province too and the private interests which suggested these projects, invested in them and also suffered major losses. It is therefore through the joint efforts of both levels of government, the private sector and the people in the area that we shall be able to gradually correct the real weaknesses of the economic structure of the Atlantic provinces. At first, we must depend on the resources, we must of course depend on the people and we must also consider future possibilities. In view of the 200-mile limit, fisheries have a fantastic potential, but we must not go too fast because we have things to do and we must do them by stages.
Because of its geographical position, Newfoundland is the province which has direct access to this resource. We are also aware of this potential, and my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) is also well aware of this potential, of certain difficulties, of certain prerequisites for an effective management of this resource, both in the short and in the long term, because it requires substantial investments on the part of the governments and the private sector.
Mr. Speaker, we could dwell a long time on what the department has done. I shall not mention any amount of money because that would be the easy way out. The statistics are available to everyone, and I shall not refer to them because I think there is something much more fundamental in the concern we should have today, namely how to co-ordinate our

efforts to be able to develop the economy of the Atlantic provinces.
I see the hon. member from Cape Breton. He will take the floor later. Of course, he will refer to the problems of the province of Nova Scotia, and to those of Cape Breton in particular. He knows my concerns very well. He is very well aware of the objectives we are trying to pursue and to fulfill at the present time. He knows very well that in the last few months we made certain decisions. We helped SYSCO to modernize. We see results. We hope that some of the things indicated to us will be confirmed and we can reasonably have some hope in that respect.
As to the energy potential which coal offers to the province of Nova Scotia, which depended so much on oil for its energy, this is obviously a fantastic asset, but we have to act according to our possibilities. Studies are being carried out and we hope they will confirm the possibility of developing a new mine sooner or later. We have been told that the reserves were substantial but a number of aspects regarding the ore contents and characteristics are still to be determined. This will be done soon but we can already assume that in the next years important investments will be made in the energy field of the Atlantic provinces because they have potential resources which will bring along, not only on a short term basis but also on a long term basis, a prosperity which has been absent for too long, although it was there unexploited in our soil, but absent in the way that it did not bring any additional wealth to maritime residents and communities.
Furthermore, the conference indicated that very soon we intended to tackle two or three projects. Several plans have already been publicized and the government has been blamed for not presenting concrete plans or proposals to the conference. We wanted all premiers attending the conference to co-operate, to have a say in the decision taking process and to identify with us the potentialities of each province. We have reached our objectives and I refer to the press release, although it gives just a part of our future decisions which will be considered by both levels of government during the next months on a number of items now under study as regards our responsibilities, on the federal side, and also the joint responsibilities of both levels of government.
I see that time is flying by, Mr. Speaker, and that you will probably ask me shortly to resume my seat. However, I would like to assure hon. members of one thing, namely that I am still pursuing the research with my officials and that I am consulting outside experts. The hon. member for Halifax referred to the Economic Council of Canada and to its report Living Together which I have read, believe me. I have discussed it. I agree with parts of it, I am not quite convinced about others but I do not necessarily reject them. I agree with some criticisms which were made, or with some positive suggestions to the effect that we should develop new tools or new means of intervention besides those which are available to DREE. Obviously we have not used up all the means of intervention, and I hope that during the next months or weeks we will have the opportunity to see new methods added to the
February 16, 1978

arsenal of tools we now have to fight disparities. We have seen a regionalization of unemployment insurance benefits, as well as a regionalization of investment credits.
The unemployment tax credit has been regionalized. This did not come by accident, it resulted from analyses and recommendations from my department as well as discussions with my colleagues so that gradually we draft our legislation on line with the plans of the Department of Finance. I believe we succeeded in breaching the wall. The principle is that Fiscal policies must pay special attention to the regions. I agree completely with the hon. member for Halifax when he said we have yet to use the fiscal instrument to its full extent. I considered many suggestions which had been put forward. I have a few ideas which I have discussed and which I continue to advocate. I hope they will be accepted, maybe not completely but in part, but they all convey recognition of a need for intervention through a national policy on a regional basis.
That is why the Prime Minister wanted DREE to participate in all those sectorial conferences in order to take into account that regional aspect in all sectorial policies. I was quite happy because my role in the federal government must be to ensure that all my colleagues in all departments are aware of the regional impact of their policy. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, I will not abuse the House's courtesy. Since I have taken all this time to speak of the Atlantic provinces, I would now like to say a few words about Quebec where serious problems are also known to exist. There are also a number of agreements in force in Quebec, nine which have been amended 17 times. They are significant and their content is more substantial than their number indicates. Sometimes I hear criticisms, as I did this week from Quebec authorities, that not enough money is being spent in Quebec on a per capita basis, and it is a fact our spending per capita is not very high in Quebec, despite what is said in certain quarters. In actual dollars, however, more money is being spent in Quebec than in other provinces. But it must be realized that in Quebec the population is very large, relatively speaking. Nevertheless the essential factor to look at is the kind of projects we are involved in.
In that province as elsewhere, we are involved in resources. Mr. Berube, the Minister of Forests who is responsible for resources, forests in particular, was complaining Wednesday morning of a lack of support. I do not believe he is absolutely
Regional Disparities
right because two agreements were signed, dealing precisely with forests. Substantial amounts have been appropriated, more than $80 million to help develop Quebec's forests. There are other substantial amounts. More than $100 million have also been appropriated for highway upgrading. We have funds earmarked for the promotion of large industries. Recently we signed an agreement for the development of industrial infrastructures for which we will be paying $46 million over and above the $36 million already invested.
We have stepped in in a rather vigorous way to help Quebec's economy, and I cannot let go unchallenged suggestions that DREE does not contribute its full share. Maybe more can be done. We will try to allocate more funds for specific projects, and I hope that during the coming weeks, the coming months, I hope to be able to get involved in specific problems and still do more in Quebec, because I recognize that an 11 per cent rate unemployment is quite intolerable. But we are prepared to do all we can provided we get the co-operation of the province of Quebec which is extremely important. I would like to point out that if Quebec would co-operate to the same extent as the other provinces, things would go much more smoothly. Ultimatums are not always the right approach.

In any case, Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude by saying that as far as Quebec is concerned, we have come forward with infrastructures as part of our ongoing auxiliary agreements which, for the federal government, now represent commitments amounting to well over $1,200 million. Some of these commitments will be spread out over the next few years. I will now make reference to industrial assistance, and I insist on dealing with that point because I know that for some of our colleagues, that aspect is more actual, more visible, especially since, as far as Quebec is concerned, that amount is proportionately larger compared to other provinces.
Every year, Quebec companies request assistance under the act providing for assistance to industries. Since Quebec has a greater number of industries, more applications inevitably are received from that province, and because of that we have to provide positive answers to a larger number of applications and, consequently, we spend more money there. It is thus normal that it be so, but if we look at the total commitments of the DREE in Quebec, I do not feel that hon. members from other parts of Canada should have any reason to say that the DREE is investing all of its money in Quebec. It is not true. We strive to balance things out. I think that we are trying to give a positive answer to all sensible applications we receive from all parts of Canada.
I should also like to conclude by saying that, last June, we designated Montreal as a special zone, effective on July 1. There again, people suggested that this system was an exercise in futility, that it did not yield the expected results. I just want to give you the figures, for I think they are significant. Since that program was implemented on February 9, we received 266 applications from private enterprises requesting assistance to expand, update or simply go into business. Of the total number of applications, decisions were made in 103 cases. Sixty-eight offers have already been forwarded to different firms. About 40 of them filed a positive answer, and the fact that the others have 90 days to reply to our proposal may account for certain delays. But everything is doing fine now, and if all those projects were to be carried out, 65 of those proposals, for instance, would require total investments of up to $50 million which would create 1,800 jobs, an end result achieved with the assistance of our total commitments of $9,500,000.
Many projects are now under consideration. In our files in Montreal, there are projects which would cost approximately

$700 million if they were all implemented. Of course, companies submit proposals which are studied, some are accepted, others are not, and in some cases they are withdrawn by the companies themselves. The complexity of this situation must be realized. I feel optimistic about the future. We will keep on promoting Quebec's economic development, we will keep on responding positively in most cases to the Quebec government's proposals as far as possible, and I am sure that in the next months, the next years, if only the Quebec government will co-operate, we will manage to lower the unemployment rate in Quebec, but it is not a federal responsibility only. I think that to create a climate favourable to investment, is also a prime responsibility of the provincial government in office. I believe that on that score the Quebec government has not always done its best in the last few months, it has not always made the appropriate statements, and judging by some statements made by the premier himself, it is certainly not the way to attract industrial investments. But we still hope there will be some, there will certainly be some investments, and we will keep on promoting the economic development of the province of Quebec, as well as the Atlantic provinces, the western provinces, the prairie provinces and British Columbia.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) for introducing this motion today. Both the hon. member for Halifax and the minister in charge of DREE made reference to efforts in the past.
We had the hon. member for Halifax making the statement that, in his opinion, the economy of the Atlantic region is relatively weaker in real terms than it was ten years ago. The minister, in an apparent attempt to meet this criticism, quoted from a statement made by the Conservative premier of New Brunswick, and he used statistics which I do not think proved his case at all. He started from a base of 1961 to 1974 and used percentage figures. That proves nothing except that he started from a lower base with his criteria, especially the criteria of fixed investment in the Atlantic region.
Then the minister made the remarkable statement that Mr. Hatfield said that if it was not for the general down-turn in the business cycle the Atlantic region would be better off. Any high school can tell him that. But this has been a traditional policy and part and parcel of the private capital market system under which we all operate. Even though it is a mixed one today because of government intervention, which was made necessary because of the decline of that system at the time of the depression in the 1930s, we have a situation in which this imbalance is built into the scheme of things. In a federal state it gives protection to the private sector in the centre of the country. When aggregate demands and the total economy keeps going down until we have a national recession, the overflow in terms of the outer region, and especially the Atlantic region, makes us that much worse off.
In that debate I would have to side strongly with the hon. member for Halifax on theoretical, empirical, and historical
February 16, 1578

grounds. The problem is that there is a recession in Canada lasting for four years. Conditions are unquestionably, in my opinion, much worse in the Atlantic procinces, than they were ten years ago, as the member for Halifax states. We know, as the minister pointed out, that the main emphasis of DREE in the Atlantic region was to support what was called a growth centre theory of development.
There are acceptable theories of development ranging from what is called an export base or an economic based theory by which exports from your area should exceed imports. By looking at a nation as a region, then we as a nation have followed this in our line of development. Most of our development has been in staple products to the neglect of a manufacturing sector that could be viable and competitive.
At one time we put too much stress on the staple primary products and at the same time over-protected the secondary manufacturing sector. The secondary manufacturing sector now cannot stand the gaff of international competition. Everyone is surprised that there is low productivity. They try to blame it on wage rates and so on. The biggest cause of the lack of productivity in this country is the built-in protection that is constantly there as a hidden subsidy to central Canada manufacturers. It's called a tariff. Therefore, it is not surprising that the Atlantic region is badly off.
To be fair to DREE, they did move into the growth areas which are the centres of government, namely Halifax in Nova Scotia, St. John's in Newfoundland, Charlottetown in Prince Edward Island and Fredericton in New Brunswick, with an overflow into Saint John which is coupled with the growth of the port in that metropolitan area. The result is very serious for outlying areas.
Recently DREE issued a document on one-industry towns and similar types of areas. It gives due recognition to these areas, but it is only a first step.
1 wish to underline the disparity noted by the hon. member for Halifax, and agreed to by the minister, between growth areas in the Atlantic region and the outlying areas. For example, in 1971, the disparity between the Halifax-Dartmouth area and the Canadian average for Canada in terms of per capita income for that area of Nova Scotia was 75 per cent of the national average. That gap has been rapidly closing and it is now closer to 85 or 90 per cent. In Cape Breton, where Sydney is the largest city, the rate was 56 per cent. In Glace Bay it was 48 per cent, and in New Waterford 46 per cent. That is according to 1971 census statistics, the only ones available. This type of information was not gathered during the 1976 census. The trend is there.
If we are going to close the gap, the allocation of human and financial resources will have to be diverted to these areas. They will have to be diverted to northern New Brunswick, the outlying areas of Newfoundland and the outlying areas of Nova Scotia. As the minister noted, Prince Edward Island is a special case because of the small geographic area and the compactness of the product markets, and the labour markets.
Regional Disparities
I do not want to criticize DREE unduly. However, it is long past time that they zeroed in on these tough areas rather than tackling the relatively easy areas in which development would occur naturally under the growth of government at the provincial level. Now is the time, I repeat, to use the financial and human resources to develop these outlying areas. Opportunities within those regions must be identified so that solid development can take place. There must be government encouragement in the way of incentives, grants and so on. It can be done.
We can look to the example of Scotland, and of parts of England and Wales. As the minister noted, this would be very difficult as well as expensive. Over a long period of time they developed areas that had been considered hopeless from the point of view of being developed. The Labour government started this regional development policy. It has not been a total success, but it has been a major effort toward closing the gaps in employment and income in that nation.
A long term look must be taken at the primary resources in the Atlantic region. As the minister stated, there is a 200-mile fishing zone. Most of us hope that consideration will soon be given to a 50-mile zone for inshore fishing. This should be done after the stocks have been built up.
We must not make the mistakes that have been made in the past. This is a prime case of a region being neglected. There has been a lack of policy by the federal and provincial governments with regard to a resource that was once looked down upon as something that was only good enough for the Newfies, the humble cod. We now know this fishery has immense potential.
Oceanographic possibilities in the Atlantic region have to some extent been recognized by the establishment of the Bedford Institute of Technology in Halifax. It is part and parcel of the whole picture. However, we have to develop more species of fish. Once the stocks are again running true to nature, we cannot just sit back without proper management and care of that resource. That would be neglecting an important part of the national economy, the Atlantic region. It has been neglected in the past as a result of failures of governments.
I can understand the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) finding it difficult to understand exactly what the maritime premiers want. Although the experts are not agreed on this, there seems to be general agreement that we are entering into an era of oil shortages, if not in the physical sense then in the sense that it will be extremely costly. Therefore we should not allocate too much of our natural resources to building huge airports and airplanes.
When one considers the extent to which the operating costs of Air Canada have increased in the past few years due to increases in the price of fuel alone, one wonders how much planning has really gone into the future of transportation-I have in mind the movement of goods and people from 1990 on, well into the next century. We ought to be putting a far

February 16, 1978
Regional Disparities
greater proportion of our resources into the development of railroads. We ought to be improving the rail beds and bringing up to date the equipment used in railway maintenance and improvement. This will all be necessary from a very practical point of view.
Alberta coal will be desperately needed in Central Canada ten or more years from now. Coal both from the east and the west will be urgently required by the Ontario steel plants and utilities. At the moment they feel secure because they have captive mines in the United States. But that coal will sooner or later run out and our own supplies are at the extremities of the country, on the west coast and on the east coast. The steel industry and the utilities, I repeat, will need that coal, so the rail lines through central Canada will need to be rebuilt. They must be rebuilt from Cape Breton Island through to Montreal and Toronto. This would do a lot, in the process, to help the hard-pressed steel industry in Nova Scotia.
The minister mentioned the recent help given to SYSCO. I was bitterly disappointed at the government's failure to take over that Sydney steel plant when it set up the Cape Breton Development Corporation after the private profit corporation, Hawker Siddeley, walked out on us. Enough studies have now been completed to justify the formation of a special body which would ask the question seriously: is there any hope of building a billion dollar industry down there which would have such a spin-off as to effect not only Cape Breton Island but Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, well into the next century? Nobody is studying such a proposition seriously. The government is content to provide dribs of assistance here and there, guaranteed loans, such as the $70 million to the Sydney steel plant and so on, is an effort to patch things up while the provincial government lumbers along running the plant inefficiently and going into the hole.
That isn't the way to use the taxpayers' money or the resources of this nation. It is not a question of ideology. The fact is, private enterprise has gone in there, communities were built up, and an infrastructure provided. Workers, along with their families, moved to these communities in large numbers. What will be our answer to the threat to this social pattern? When will we be prepared to ask ourselves the question: is it or is it not economically possible under government auspices, with proper management, to build an international, competitive steel plant in the Atlantic region? When will we let the people know, once and for all, what is in store? We cannot act simply as politicians all the time thinking of the short run. That is the lesson of the first ministers' conference. The purposes of this country continue beyond four years. Many of the problems which face us today are those from decisions made by other groups of politicians in the past and taken with only short term advantage in mind.
