subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
I thank hon. members for allowing me an extra few minutes. A great deal has already been said on the subject of energy, and I am sure much more will be said by hon. members like the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) with regard to energy development in the Atlantic region based on Fundy tides and the increasing use of our coal reserves both in the east and in Alberta.
The minister did mention coal. The potential for this form of energy in Nova Scotia was written off in the short run some years ago. But that was before the Arabs came out of their tents and formed the OPEC monopoly. The situation now is that a great deal of money will have to be spent on the development of our coal resources since there are literally billions of tons of coal in this country which can either be burned or put to other commercial uses. The primary need, in the east, is for $ 16 million to be spent in Glace Bay refurbishing a coal mine, No. 26, which produces coal of the highest grade with only a very low sulphur content. Indeed, conditions are right at the present time for the reopening of two further collieries. Even though we still need DREE, I would make the following suggestions, bearing in mind the constraints we face in the need to get elected or re-elected every few years and the fact that governments cannot hope to achieve much success by short term solutions which are often not solutions at all.
In the long run, a new institution is needed to probe deeply into the actual and potential resource base of the Atlantic region. I am referring to the physical, primary resource base, excluding the manufacturing and service sectors. As I have mentioned before, some of this is ongoing at the present time in specialized agencies such as the Oceanographic Institute at Bedford in Halifax.
It would be worth while to consider having a body composed of permanent members of the Science Council of Canada, representatives of the Secretariat of Maritime Premiers, a representative of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Maritimes Chambers of Commerce. These members could be appointed on a biannual or triannual basis. Also there should be representatives from labour federations of Atlantic Canada, as well as one or two members from the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. Also there should be one or two members from the Atlantic universities as such. It would be strictly a non-political body. Both the federal and provincial governments would provide funds. Its major function would be to examine in depth long term technical and economic feasibilities for maritimes primary resource development. Its secondary function would be to attempt to improve the coordination of present existing long range federal and provincial policies for development of the Atlantic region. I propose that such an institution be called "The Atlantic Provinces Research
Regional Disparities
and Study Institute for Long Term Development of Atlantic Canada's Primary Resources".
I make that suggestion because it is in that direction that our future prosperity lies in the Atlantic region, despite the fact the other sectors have a relatively important part to play in our future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) for the very interesting motion which he has moved. It deals with actual present-day problems. I am very much concerned about the problems in the Atlantic provinces, as they are similar to the ones we have on the south shore. This is the reason why I want to congratulate the hon. member for the thrust of his motion in dealing with these specific problems.
The population of the constituency of Bellechasse, which I have the honour to represent in this House, represents 1.37 per cent of the overall population of Quebec. And yet, the manufacturing sector accounts for only .75 per cent of the whole of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, this question of regional disparities has to do with the inadequacy of industrial development which does not allow people to find jobs or earn a normal living in their own province. On the other hand, while 1.8 per cent of Quebec's factories are located in the constituency of Bellechasse, only 0.8 per cent of the factory workers are employed there.
The fact that most industries, in this area, are not big plants but small and medium-sized companies accounts for this disparity. Industries prefer being located closer to our larger cities and to the large North American markets. They could hardly be blamed because in the present state of things, those industries seek primarily to minimize their costs and we know that freight rates would only add to the manufacturing cost of their products and make them less competitive.
A logical solution to this problem would be to grant a special transport subsidy to companies which would be ready to move to outlying areas, far from our major centres. That would be one way of eliminating one of the factors contributing to the concentration of industries in already well-developed areas.
Earlier I heard the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) mention the many benefits that have already been made available. I agree that this led to improvements but the evidence shows that it was not enough. I thank him for what has already been done but I ask him to do even more. If we have intensive development we will be able to maintain in our areas at least the level of population we now have and this will make it easier to lighten the burden of public expenditures for those who must live in those areas. The more people we have, the fairer the distribution.
In a given region it is important and logical to look for industries which have historically been related to it but which have experienced difficult times over the years. An example

February 16, 1978
Regional Disparities
that comes to mind is the Davie Ship Building yards in Lauzon which have been a large employer in my area for a long time; even if it is in Lauzon many workers from the ridings of Bellechasse and Montmagny earn their living there.
In think an expansion of the yard in Lauzon would provide many jobs so the people in that area would be able to get organized, be more economically active and have less need to fall back on governments to remain afloat. Last week I heard the motion of the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) urging the government to give very special attention to the possibility of establishing a Canadian merchant marine. It is not the first time this matter is being raised in the House.
I too had an opportunity to introduce a motion along those lines. I think the last time I introduced such a motion was last Monday when I urged the House to set up a special committee to consider the advantages of using the millions of dollars we are now paying in the form of subsidies for building ships, very often to foreign businesses. This has an advantage. The government has done its best with this policy to protect the level of employment, and in 1976-77, the government paid $65 million in grants to 45 companies. $65 million is quite a lot of money. If we tried to use part of this sum to develop a merchant marine, we would also create employment, but at the same time we would be giving Canada a very important economic tool.
I remember reading a few years ago that at a certain time Canada was the third largest owner of merchant ships in the world. I wonder why we did not continue to support our merchant marine which made us dependent upon foreign companies for our coastal trade. This is certainly a profitable industry since I have never known one of those foreign companies to go bankrupt. They buy ships, they rebuild them, make them seaworthy and then they have a profitable transportation trade.
With regard to the mode of transportation to which I alluded earlier, I have already suggested in the House that a study be made on the transportation of goods by truck or rail between the most easterly point of the country and Montreal to find out what are the actual difficulties and why companies are not able to continue their operations let alone to expand. Under Bill C-ll tax benefits of lxh per cent are provided for companies in the maritimes and the Gaspe area, but the South Shore area, which also needs this assistance was forgotten. The IVi per cent benefit was increased to 10 per cent, but still, all the South Shore companies were forgotten even though they greatly need this assistance. I once again bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) so that he may make representations to his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), who could perhaps amend Bill C-ll to allow these companies to take advantage of these tax benefits.
Mr. Speaker, a while ago I heard the minister quote the agreements made with the provinces, including the province of Quebec, and the benefits involved. I am very happy about this

and I would like these means of communication between the various levels of governments to continue and to improve. However, Mr. Speaker, since we have a very high level of unemployment in our area, I believe that the time has come to extend these agreements or to draw up a special agreement for the South Shore area. Yesterday, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) what progress had been made in the negotiations concerning the transfer of certain communication wharves between Ottawa and Quebec. He was somewhat reluctant to give me an answer. Today, the situation has improved and I have been assured that exchanges are going on and that results will soon be achieved. There again, if there was an agreement to help speed up the building of communication wharves and upgrade them, jobs could be created, while capital projects were being carried out and a problem solved. In Montmagny, in the cove, and I am sure the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion knows what I am talking about, there is an tremendous location to build a marina. People have wanted a marina there for years, and nature has provided us with all those opportunities.
Therefore I hope that with Bill C-2 introduced by the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), it would be possible to achieve that objective. But as the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion put it so well a moment ago, it often takes the co-operation of two, three or four departments to succeed in achieving an objective. So, while building that marina, it would also be necessary to provide for new highway programs in order to allow easier access to it and to develop the tourist industry, which would be of great benefit not only to the city of Montmagny but also to the whole area.
There is another suggestion I would like to make. Bellechasse is a very beautiful riding. When you travel south to the U.S. border, you see beautiful mountains there and it would be possible to set up a flourishing tourist industry in that area. Farming cannot be further developed and I do not believe we should leave that immense territory unused. Today I received a letter once again from a local resident who asked me if there was a program of federal assistance to help entrepreneurs put up businesses and breed fish by building small dams across the rivers. This would not only create employment directly and allow local people to get involved but it would mean producing goods and selling them. That is the way to create industries and jobs. Of course I had to answer that such a program did not exist at the moment but there is nothing stopping us from implementing one in the future.
So, I think it would be possible to develop that kind of program in that area which would benefit economically, financially and socially. I also wish to draw the minister's attention to the crucial problem of the textile industry. There are textile plants in our area. Again this week I received a brief from three textile companies asking me to press for more specific protection measures. This brief mentioned not the Kennedy Round but the Tokyo Round. I was also sent a newspaper article entitled: "Investments in the United States, Joblessness in Canada." This report is supported by figures showing that this is absolutely true. We should negotiate better trading
February 16, 1978

terms and conditions to protect those industries which are no more inefficient than the others. They have all the facilities to produce. They have good equipment, modern looms and the quality of their product is excellent. Elowever, they have difficulty to make ends meet. But they manage to survive. Salaries are not high but adequate. Of course, it might be cheaper to live on the other side of the border, I do not know, I have never lived there but subsidized transportation and tax cuts would help them tremendously. This is why I ask that this area be included among those who will receive tax rebates; it would help enormously.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding, I would also like to quote from an article published in the February 9 issue of Le Devoir. It says: "Provinces invited to increase deficit". This was at the very centre of the federal-provincial conference that was held earlier this week: each government wants to do great things, each one is extremely willing, but none has enough revenues to meet its responsibilities. That is why the Prime Minister is reported to have said: "The provinces should increase their deficit". But our national deficit will reach the $9 billion mark this year, and this is an increase of $5 billion over last year's deficit which was of $4 billion. All these governments, both at the federal and provincial levels, are caught in a vicious cycle, to say the least. What does the future hold in store for us? We are not accumulating these enormous debts because of any war nor because of any natural catastrophe. How is it that competent and intelligent Canadian management ends up advocating such methods or solutions for Canadian financing in 1978?
Mr. Speaker, we must call a spade a spade: a $9 billion deficit is tantamount to an indebtedness imposed upon our future generations. But if we have a $9 billion deficit, we must borrow money somewhere to write it off. That is why I feel this is our big chance. We must take advantage of our economic and financial difficulties and carry out a reform of our methods of financing the public sector. Never will I relent on this issue, for I am convinced that this reform is a necessity, and as long as we do not get it done, we shall get deeper and deeper into debt. We shall be dragging down with us the provinces, the municipalities, the school boards, and also, indirectly, the Canadian taxpayers who will have to pay higher rates and higher taxes in order to pay up the interests on these debts which are increasing at a frightening pace.
As a matter of fact, the purpose of Bill C-390 which is now before the House is to increase the powers of the Bank of Canada. Which way? Precisely to prevent us from getting deeper into debt next year by another $9 billion, but how? Nobody knows. I, for one, recommend that the Bank of Canada Act be amended to make it possible for the Bank of Canada to grant long-term loans to the federal government. We would undertake to refund these loans to the Bank of Canada in the same way as we refund other loans to our other creditors, but at least, we would be owing that money to ourselves, because the Bank of Canada is ours. In this way, we
Regional Disparities
would be borrowing from our own institution moneys which we would then have to reimburse, but not at the high interest rates that we are required to pay now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite happy to take part in this opposition day debate since the subject is most interesting for all Canadians and especially for those living in our own areas of the country with which we are particularly concerned. Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield). I am quite happy to participate in this debate because it gives me a chance to speak in this House on a subject which concerns me very much and which is of vital interest to Quebec, that is, regional disparities.
Furthermore, I am honored to echo the well thought-out statement made earlier by the former leader of my party, the hon. member for Halifax, a man who has been denouncing and fighting regional disparities throughout his career, both on the provincial and federal scene. If we had listened more to him at that time, perhaps our country would not be today in so much trouble and difficulty, because the hon. member for Halifax has been talking about discussion, cooperation and consultation for a long time.
I also wish to add a few remarks to the speech made by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard). He acknowledge, much to my pleasure, the objectivity of the statements and proposals made by the hon. member for Halifax. He also acknowledged some valid recommendations, ad I know that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is able to do this with enough objectivity. He also mentioned the federal provincial conference where a great many good intentions were shown. He spoke of the co-operation that is essential with the provinces and with Quebec, and demonstrated, of course, his good will with regard to the efforts his government is willing to make, in view of the problems we know.
I should also like to point out that his department is in fact directly involved in the interests of several ridings, of which mine that benefited from a subsidiary agreement granting it special privileges related to certain investments taking into account the type of industries that may be entitled to those subsidies. I understand, of course, that it would probably have been impossible for all types of industries to benefit from them. Recently I was very happy to learn that a $1 million agreement was signed with the province of Quebec, through which my riding will benefit from an infrastructure for an industrial park that is already quite well installed, but still needs money to attract more industry.
So, Mr. Speaker, I really do not question the good faith or good will of the minister. Before him, when the department was set up, there were times, to my mind, when it was not as well intentioned as the minister seemed to explain to us today. I am sure that because of the situation, the federal government feels compelled to do more consulting and be more understanding of the provinces.
Now, I should like to say a few words about the federal-provincial conference. The minister responsible stressed the

February 16, 1978
Regional Disparities
importance of speaking the truth, and I feel, it must be spoken in the Elouse. I say this in a positive vein. I should therefore like to invite him, particularly, and knowing that he is capable of doing so, to show more interest than ever before in the province in which I live, as many others do, and especially, not to allow himself to be influenced by some of his colleagues who, whether we like it or not, Mr. Speaker, at times have some difficulty in accepting the recommendations of the Quebec government.
The minister pointed out the dramatic situation in which the province of Quebec finds itself. He recognized, I believe, the importance of giving it a hand. I think it is the duty of the government, of his department, and like him, I have surely no hesitation in promoting a sincere co-operation and consultation and also in urging that province to keep within the limits and criteria set in the legislation. We should seriously consider the possibility of showing to the people in Quebec that the economic climate can and should be restored with the co-operation of the federal government. I am quite pleased to see that the minister has stressed that co-operation so much and I feel that he has truly shown its good faith.
Once again 1 invite him to exert his influence on some of his colleagues who may not show the same objectivity as he does or may not be able as he is to overcome sectarian opinions to take a real interest in the welfare and legitimate aspirations of the province of Quebec. I am confident that the minister will be able to fulfil the commitments he has taken today and, as a Quebecker, I hope he will do so and I am going to do my best to invite the government and the people of Quebec to show the same goodwill in order to promote the industrial development which has been so badly missed by the people of Quebec until now.
In another vein, Mr. Speaker, in the opening speech the Prime Minister delivered at the conference on Monday, he said at the very beginning that Canadians felt concerned about our present situation and, in the same breath, he added that the unemployment and inflation rates will soon be brought to an acceptable level and that the economic recovery was already well under way, that the conference was the beginning of a continuing consultation between the federal government and the provinces and that, all in all, everything was going well in the best of worlds.
Mr. Speaker, I have never seen the government so open to this type of consultation and good will. We must nevertheless ask ourselves: how is it that in the last ten years we have not felt this deep desire for co-operation and consultation with the provinces such as we have seen in the last few days. They chose to let the provinces choke, and then call up on them to make recommendations, suggestions. However, I have followed closely the federal-provincial conference where the government, echoing some well-known publicity slogans, simply asked the provinces: Now, what can we do for you? Ottawa is on your side and it's good for you. We hardly accept newspaper reports suggesting that for some premiers such a campaign

had a pre-election flavour to it. We cannot accept that this idea may have come through their minds!
Mr. Speaker, I am not saying that this conference should not have taken place, as there are rumours about forthcoming elections. Yet I think, like many others, that it should have been held a year ago. Either the government did not hold it last year because it was not aware of the dangers threatening us and of the urgent need for such a conference, which seems to indicate irresponsibility or incompetence, or the government realized that on the eve of general elections it had better get the provinces together and present them with problems that he was already aware of, and know would grow worse, because in this way, the federal government knew it could expect a more favourable response to the well intentioned proposals it had been making over these past three days.
1 nevertheless hope that the present co-operative spirit shown by the provinces will be matched by a serious effort of coordination on the part of the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, to be truthful, we must admit that it is some sort of a farce when the prime minister feels all he has to do is state that the economic recovery is already under way, which I am not so sure about. I am inclined to think that there has been a wanton abuse of words and media coverage for electoral purposes. The truth is that Canadians are concerned and have every reason to be, even though those concerns were played down at the conference. What is not true is as the present government would have us believe that the people's concern is due to the wickedness of the government's opponents and propagated by the negative remarks of the media in search of striking headlines.
The fact, Mr. Speaker, is that there are over a million unemployed in Canada and it is not the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) who is saying that, or even some premier, but Statistics Canada. It is even so much of a fact that according to impartial observers, unemployment went beyond the size of a problem to become some kind of a national disgrace. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, inflation has reached the 9 per cent level which is much higher than in the United States and one of the highest among developed countries, although controls were established in 1975. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had laughed them off when our party advocated them during the 1974 campaign, but he later implemented them, too late however and without adequate consultation, without an overall plan arrived at with the provinces and interested sectors. Those same inadequate controls that let inflation reach its current level, are to be lifted on April 14, and we may wonder what will happen then. The fact also is that according to the Economic Council of Canada our economy, although capable of sustaining a 5 per cent annual growth, only attained half that goal last year. Forecasts by economists outside the government are to the effect that we will not do much better in 1978. The fact is, that today some 18 per cent of our producing capacity is unused; however the government is sufficiently wrapped up in its bureaucratic red tape to suggest that we should avoid too hasty a recovery for fear that it might revive inflation. The fact is also, Mr. Speaker, that last year we paid
February 16, 1978

out in unemployment insurance benefits alone more than $4 billion while during that same period we lost at least $7 billion in potential production Canadians could have put out had they had jobs. Another fact is that our Canadian dollar is faltering, our exports are declining, our balance of payments is increasing at an alarming rate, our budget deficits are getting bigger and bigger, our national debt on a per capita basis continues to increase and reliable sources throughout the world are beginning to cast doubts about the Canadian government's economic capability. In the meantime investors at home have lost confidence for at least four years, they are investing more and more abroad, consumers themselves have become diffident and purchases are on a constant decline. Such are the facts, Mr. Speaker. What concerns the Canadian people at this time is this government's economic performance. Mind you, we might as well be prepared because it is against this background that lies the shape of things to come.
Some businessmen might be impressed by such a management of the economy but I presume that those businessmen are not that impressed. As for me, I hope for something far better to serve my country and I do not want to be told that another government could not do any better. The only way to find out would be to try it, Mr. Speaker. Faced with that failure of the present administration, the Prime Minister in his opening statement before the provincial conference once again resorted to his old trick of comparing the performance of the Canadian economy with those of other countries. That prompted a few people to say that the Prime Minister wanted us to believe that everything was fine in the worst of worlds. But speaking of confidence, Mr. Speaker, it is certainly not with the performance of the present government that one can regain the confidence of Canadian voters or of members on this side of the House who have once too often heard completely erroneous forecasts and projections. And to what extent have we been misled, to what extent have they proved to be incompetent and irresponsible in making forecasts?
But for ten years, Mr. Speaker, millions of dollars have been swallowed up in all sorts of more or less worth-while plans and structures which rarely become reality, millions of dollars which could have been invested in employment producing projects.
The hon. member for Halifax said earlier that five or six years ago, if I remember well, in a tour he made across this country he warned this government of the dangers which were facing us. He said about regional disparities that we had to deal with the problem in a rational way and not with temporary solutions as this government has done. I do not question what the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion said today-what he said in the House today is entirely new and encouraging for that matter, I must admit-but I would like very much his predecessors and his government to think like him, that before they set up regional economic policy they establish in close co-operation with the provinces a national economic policy and then see how provincial and regional needs can be fitted into that policy. It is in that contact that we
Regional Disparities
advocated during the 1972 campaign the calling as soon as possible of a conference on tomorrow's priorities.
What I am recalling for the benefit of the House today, Mr. Speaker, is exactly what the hon. member for Halifax who was then the leader of the Progressive Conserative party advocated years ago, and it is exactly what this government refused to hear, with the results that we now know. At present, the government is moving on regional economic expansion, as in other areas, without co-ordination and planning. So he referred to it earlier-this is new. That gave the results we know when we saw plants receive federal subsidies to promote regional economies and those very plants closed their doors a few months later.
The problem of regional disparities is not an easy one to solve. We admit that but I suggest that this party could do a lot better and would have already brought about solutions. When we get to form the government, and the time will come, we will carry out a complete review of all those regional development and economic expansion programs, in consultation of course with provincial governments and the people in underprivileged area. We are also going to launch a massive attack on all fronts where the problems lie, the effects of which will inevitably be felt in the area of regional disparities. This coherent offensive will simultaneously deal with problems of unemployment, cost of living, economic growth, taxation and housing. Allow me to point out some of those measures and if we had been called to govern the country, we would also have created the proposed investment funds to stimulate small businesses and new jobs would already be available here and there.
We realize the incompetence and clumsiness of the federal government, because for too long it has refused to coordinate its policies; it has invested huge amounts in the economics of areas where transport is primitive and shipping costs are almost prohibitive. I think that transport is also a very important question. I would like to say that with a government which is allegedly respectful of regional economic growth, we should have a national transport policy to cope with deficiencies and disparities. In spite of all the projects and plans devised by bureaucrats in their ivory towers, up to recent times, regional disparities have remained one of the main problems in Canada. They are a major problem more specifically because they threaten the success of our confederation and at the same time, they are in a certain way a negation of the concept on which it is based. It is not necessary to be an economic expert to understand that slow growth areas are the first to feel the effects of an economic recession and the last to recover. The hon. member for Halifax has pointed out that danger quite well. As I would like to give my colleagues the opportunity to make a few comments, I wish, before concluding, that the statements made today by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion will give way to some genuine short-term action.
This afternoon, my party leader asked the right hon. Prime Minister not exactly but approximately how many new jobs would be created under the projects or objectives which the

Yet, during this federal-provincial conference, he asked the Canadian public to trust the federal government, a government which has failed in practically all areas and in connection with all the objectives he has been advocating since 1968, from the just society to the control of wages and prices, the fight against inflation and unemployment. How can he ask the Canadian public to trust a government with such an extensive and diverse record of failures. We still hope nevertheless and we shall continue to demand that the consultations which the minister in charge hoped for today become a reality, and he shall then be assured of co-operation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to participate in this motion which has been moved by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield). He has had great experience both in this House and as leader of a party for many years.
I had the opportunity to attend the first ministers' conference, and it was interesting to note the support the first ministers lent to DREE, and how necessary they find that it continues. I would like to compliment my colleague the minister responsible for DREE for the effort he is putting forth. It is a worthy instrument, especially for the part of Canada where I come from. We have many needs in the Atlantic provinces. It is difficult sometimes to determine what the picture would have been like if we had not had DREE. I will spend a few moments later on discussing how the comprehensive develop-
February 16, 1978

ment plan functions in Prince Edward Island. As hon. members know, this has been a necessary plan for Prince Edward Island.
During discussions at the first ministers' conference there was some constructive criticism, which we found beneficial. There were some suggestions for changes in emphasis which might be explored. There was also overwhelming support for the basic approach and the principal program instruments of the department. The mechanism, in particular, received favourable comment as the kind of mechanism needed to ensure a co-ordinated federal-provincial approach to economic development.
This support was reflected in the official communique issued by the first ministers at the end of the conference. The two related conclusions set forth were firstly, that the first ministers strongly affirmed the importance of reducing regional disparities and the continuing need for review and expansion of programs for regional development based on the longer run economic potential and transportation requirements of each province and region. Secondly, it was agreed DREE should continue to be a major federal agency for those purposes.
In light of developments at the first ministers' conference, it is obvious that the federal and provincial governments have renewed their commitment to regional economic development. We can be assured, therefore, that part of this motion has already been dealt with in a rather impressive way.
The motion also refers to comprehensive strategies for economic development. I certainly have no objection to this reference as long as we have in mind a workable concept. The statements of strategy already imbedded in the general development agreement are based on a workable concept. They carry the support of both senior levels of government and they are subject to regular review in light of changing circumstances. Indeed, one of the important elements of the GDA system is the provision made for annual meetings of the responsible federal and provincial ministers, meetings at which it is possible to review strategic questions, monitor progress being achieved by way of specific subsidiary agreements and make concrete plans for the period ahead.
The motion also refers to eastern Canada, suggesting a need for priority attention to the developmental requirements of eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. That part of Canada is, of course, already receiving priority under the DREE program and under various other policy instruments of the federal government. The Atlantic provinces are subject to a higher maximum than other designated regions under the Regional Development Incentives Act. The Gaspe region of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces are also subject to the newly-announced employment tax credit. In many other ways, under the programs of various federal departments and agencies, everything possible is being done to maximize the economic impact of government activity in these same regions.
I would like to say a few words about Prince Edward Island.

speechtext:
Where is that?
Regional Disparities

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
It is on this side of Newfoundland. When flying to Newfoundland, you come to Prince Edward Island first. Most members of this House realize there is a comprehensive development plan in Prince Edward Island. It is for a 15-year period and began in 1969. It is the only province in Canada that has a comprehensive plan that deals with practically every aspect of development. To my knowledge, this is not so in other provinces. The minister can correct me if I am wrong.
Its purpose is to further the economic and social development of Prince Edward Island. Approximately $225 million was spent in the plan's first phase, 1969 to 1975, to establish a sound foundation for agriculture, fishing and tourism. In addition, the education system was reorganized and schools were consolidated, major improvements were made to the highway system, housing standards were improved, and marketing facilities were strengthened. During this period the economy showed a marked improvement as employment advanced, population increased, and per capita income growth exceeded expectations.
In 1975 the second phase of the plan was introduced, placing greater emphasis on the economic sectors of the province as programs were designed to make use of the improved capacity of the province to respond to development opportunities.
In March 1977 the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) and Premier Alex Campbell signed an agreement on the financial arrangements for the remaining three years of the second phase of the comprehensive development plan. This agreement provides for a contribution by DREE of $89 million over the next three years and a continuation of the phase II strategy. Programs implemented under this agreement are cost-shared on a 90-10 federal-provincial ratio, except for school construction, which is 50-50. Emphasis will continue to be placed on the productive sectors: agriculture, fisheries, and industrial development.
I wish to mention a few other items. One is of recent construction. I refer to the submarine cable link between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. A 13.5 miles, $36 million electric cable stretching across Northumberland Strait between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island was officially opened in Charlottetown on October 28, 1977. This project began in 1969 to ease Prince Edward Island'., energy problems by linking the province to a maritime electrical grid. With a grant of $18 million from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, a $9 million loan from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources and $9 million from the Prince Edward Island government, a pair of cables manufactured in Sweden were laid into pre-dug trenches at the bottom of the Strait between Murray Corner, New Brunswick and Richmond Cove, Prince Edward Island.
The link will not lower the cost of electricity to Prince Edward Islanders but it will slow down the accelerating rate of increase. Although the Island will not draw all its power from the cable, its energy future is no longer tied to fossil fuels and to costs beyond its ability to control. The cable will be oper-

February 16, 1978
Regional Disparities
ated by Maritime Electric Co., Ltd. under lease by the Prince Edward Island government.
There are a few matters on which I would like to elaborate. I wish to make reference to how DREE is operating in Prince Edward Island and to what I feel it has accomplished.
With regard to electrical power, I know there are some in this House who will argue that we do not have the highest electrical bills in Canada. Some of my hon. friends from Newfoundland claim that. However, we are very dependent on oil. This cable is one of the great benefits we have received. It has not decreased our electricity cost, but it is a measure of security. As years pass and there is further development with water power and so on, this will be a very good thing for us.
I wish to make reference to school construction in Prince Edward Island under the development plan. We have a school system like other rural provinces which is rather spread out. Our pupils were attending one-room schools. With the help of DREE, we were able to proceed much more rapidly with consolidating schools, both secondary and high schools. This is a great benefit to us. This is one of the first programs of a comprehensive nature that was developed between the federal government and the provincial government of P.E.I. I think the minister will agree that it was used as a model at that time. However, a lot of things have come and gone since 1969.
Something else that has been very fruitful and beneficial to our province and copied in other provinces is the family farm program. I have a few more comments I would like to make, Mr. Speaker; therefore I will call it six o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the House rose at six o'clock I was concluding my remarks about DREE as applied to Prince Edward Island. I might say something now about the family farm program and the benefits derived from it.
As hon. members realize, Prince Edward Island being an agricultural province, the agricultural sector is a very important one. If it were not for DREE, those who live in the farm community in Prince Edward Island and who are able to enjoy some benefit from that program would be in a much worse position than they are at the present time. I am not trying to leave the impression that everything is cream and peaches, but I was closely associated with this scheme at its inception and I worked with it for a number of years, and I will do everything in my power to see that it is carried on and that worthwhile projects are forthcoming.

I might add that the arrangement for reviewing these programs is an excellent one. There is provision for an annual review by a joint advisory board consisting of representatives of both the provincial and federal governments.
Another area in which the government help very much is that of transportation, chiefly through road surfacing and construction. In P.E.I. we probably have more miles of road per capita than any other province. A great deal is demanded of roads today, truck traffic from one province to another being so heavy, so here again I think we would be in a bad position had it not been for federal assistance in highway construction, particularly in the maintenance of the trans-Canada highway.
The fishery is another important sector in our province. Our most lucrative fish is the lobster which brings in many dollars. It is a delicacy sold in many parts of Canada and it is likely that many people come to Prince Edward Island just to eat lobster. My other Atlantic colleagues appreciate this fish also. The government assists in the processing and in the maintenance of freezing units around harbours. Consideration is being given to using DREE money for the construction of boats also.
Something relatively new is taking place in our province. It is known as industrial malls. Industrial malls started in Charlottetown about two years ago through the efforts of the provincial government. What they really do is assist people interested in business. The province itself has a structure in this regard that is assisted through DREE in training and in implementation. When an individual gets to know his business he has an opportunity to expand and often moves on to something else. Someone then starting up in the business will take up the gap in that area.
This has proved to be very successful in this part of the country. There are over 20 in the town of Charlottetown. These employ quite a number of people and it looks like a very good thing to do for the future. The island population is small and there is no sense trying to take on big projects. Actually I think probably this is a return to our yesteryear when the people in our province, and other provinces as well, depended more or less on self-help, doing a great many things for themselves. This is something that looks very encouraging. It is expanding now to another town in Prince Edward Island, the town of Summerside, and we are looking forward to achievements in that area. As the saying goes, nothing is perfect at the onset. We are learning by our mistakes and other parts of Canada will perhaps also learn from some of the mistakes we make.
This is far, far from being all a mistake because there is enough good coming from it that it is bringing our population back. There has been a population change in the last number of years in our province. People used to say in the past that we were more or less an incubator for other parts of Canada. That is very true, but if all our people had stayed with their large families of yesteryear there would not be standing room now and they would have to leave anyway.
February 16, 1978

A lot has also been done in respect to market development. This is also assisted through DREE in conjunction with the provincial governments. Much is done in advertising and in processing, and this has been quite a help to us. Until we can get into the position in this great country of ours of having more control of production and marketing there will be some problems.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the agricultural sector depends on many things, chiefly the elements. It depends on how much rainfall we have, how much frost there is on some occasions, and how long the growing season is. These are uncontrollable factors, but you do what you can in other areas, such as in promotion, salesmanship and what have you, and this has proved very successful. What we are producing for export are goods in very highly competitive fields. Our products must be very competitive in outside markets, not just in Canada but throughout the world.
Food processing is certainly coming into its own and is highly productive in Prince Edward Island. We have a great potato crop. In the last couple of years we have processed as much as 20 per cent of our potato crop, and that is a lot of potatoes when you consider they are produced on approximately 50,000 acres. This also helps our cash receipts. As the House knows, cash receipts from potatoes have been very, very good. They are not too good this year but last year we enjoyed possibly one of the best in many, many years. This was because in times of drought, as in Europe last year, our production was more saleable.
There are aspects of DREE that assist us in many ways. Going back to the agricultural sector again, one thing that has been very fruitful and beneficial is the potato packaging scheme. We get assistance in that regard through job creation, and assistance for structures. These are all things that help keep people abreast of things and we find this very beneficial.
At one time not too many years in the past, as everyone knows, in our small province we had one of the best forestry stands in the country. It has deteriorated now a long way from that state. One of the chief reasons for this deterioration results from the actions of some human beings. When you cut the perimeter around a very small area like this and expose it to the wind, the rains, the salt spray, and what have you, it has a very bad effect on the forest. Through help from DREE and the provincial government we now have a replanting process, and the day will come when we may have our forests back to the stands that once existed. This is not something that will happen very rapidly because it takes 30 years to grow a tree for pulp and 60 years to make good lumber, so to get a good stand of lumber right across the whole island will take practically a century.
I see, Mr. Speaker, you getting ready to stand so I think I should conclude on that point. There are many more things I could speak about regarding DREE and its benefits in Prince Edward Island and in the Atlantic provinces generally. I want to endorse DREE in every way. Being a landlubber in the past I know what the situation was and can see the good that DREE has done for our province. I want to compliment the
Regional Disparities
minister for his patience and for the very intricate deals he has worked out for the Atlantic provinces. I wish him as well as our province great luck.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the hon. member of the NDP, but I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this motion. I commend the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) for introducing it, and also the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) for his contribution in producing this motion, which is significantly timely and in line with the economic conference we witnessed with great national interest over the past few days.
I watched a good deal of the economic conference and what struck me was the fact that everything I heard and read in the papers that were produced appeared to be repetition of things we have heard in the House of Commons over past years. They were the same suggestions and the same solutions to problems. I can only reflect and deduce that the provincial premiers have been reading Hansard over the past years in order to produce these papers.
Another thing struck me as I observed the conference. I wondered what our job was as federal members of parliament representing 264 districts in this place and where is the liaison between ourselves and the provinces. What has happened to the thrust we are trying to make here in the House of Commons as representatives of all Canada? What has happened to the liaison that would permit us to make those representations that should be made to the government? I can only come to the conclusion that some people are not listening to us. I wonder what we are doing here.
Certainly there must be some positive aspects about the discussions that take place between representatives of the provinces and whoever it may be that is interested in this country. I hope we will see some positive results from this conference. As I watched I heard the same cliches we have all heard for years, such as that we have to provide a climate of opportunity; we have to direct more attention to the private and, in some cases, the public sectors; we have to provide direction in the area of restraint on spending. The one that struck me the most was the suggestion that we had to instil a renewal of confidence on the part of our people and the business sector in the government.
It is a well-known fact that our citizens have lost faith in the government, but you cannot instil confidence in the people we are representing by sitting around a table repeating political cliches. You instil confidence in the people and in business by performance, by action, by leadership and by deed. We keep hearing the same problems and the same suggestions year in and year out, yet we have the same distressing situation regarding the economy of Canada, this country which we all know is so prosperous.
Our motion today relates in a few words just what the government must do immediately. It states:
-the government must now renew its commitment to reduce regional disparities by developing and implementing . . . comprehensive development strategies for

February 16, 1978
Regional Disparities
eastern Quebec and the Atlantic provinces including such areas as transportation, energy, primary resources, industrial and service sector expansion.
I want to attempt to address my remarks to these areas as they concern my province of Newfoundland.
As a result of my basic military training, I have learned some fundamental lessons. One such lesson was that any advancing army, organization, element or province can move no faster than the slowest or weakest troops. Nothing is more true when that principle is applied to our nation's economic and social direction. Canada will never reach its potential unless the weakest provinces are strengthened to keep pace with the richer ones.
Another fundamental lesson was: in order to maintain progress and win a victory, one must reinforce his success. One must take advantage of his potential strengths and reinforce them for the benefit of all. Newfoundland's strength is in its richness of renewable resources: forests, potential energy, fish, offshore oil, potential mineral resources, tourism, and most important, human resource. In spite of this richness, and in spite of joining confederation in 1949 in order to take advantage of federal leadership, Newfoundland is still embarrassingly categorized as one of the poorest provinces. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been put into Newfoundland by the government for the purpose of development. Yet it still has the highest unemployment rate and cost of living. This is partly because our leaders never developed a long term strategy in order to take advantage of the province's potential, other than on a hit and miss basis. No infrastructure base was provided, which was the first unforgiveable mistake. An adequate transportation system is a fundamental necessity to reach the rich resources of Newfoundland and Labrador.
In spite of that known fact, it probably has the most inadequate rail lines and deteriorated highways in all of Canada. The Canadian National Railways has the responsibility of maintaining its rail lines. It has allowed those lines to deteriorate to the point where they are no longer in use. The CN has turned more and more to trailer trucks in an attempt to compete in the market. That contributes greatly to the deterioration of the province's highways. The cheapest form of transportation, from an energy point of view, is the rail lines, but that is not recognized. The transportation link requires upgrading and strengthening, yet the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) refuses to offer any more than 50 per cent of the cost. Certainly the Newfoundland government cannot afford it.
I commend the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) who is providing 90 per cent of the construction cost for a highway to the Great Northern Peninsula. That highway is 1 hg constructed to take advantage of the resources whiv are in northern Newfoundland and Labrador. How can one minister offer only 50 per cent of the cost while another minister is providing 90 per cent of the cost of the Great Northern Peninsula highway? The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion recognizes the value of Newfoundland's
resources. Originally the federal government assisted in the construction of the Trans-Canada Highway on a 90-10 basis. In order to take advantage of the resources which can be found in the Great Northern Peninsula, northern Newfoundland and Labrador, work must be done on the Trans-Canada Highway from Port aux Basques to the jump-off point in the triangle of Deer Lake, Corner Brook and St. Stephen.
I should like to refer to some statistics which were prepared by the trucking associations of the Atlantic provinces. Between 1970 and 1976, rail transportation increased by 3 per cent. It was an increase from 385,000 tons to 397,000 tons. Truck and trailer traffic increased by 424 per cent. Thus, it must be fundamentally obvious that the highway has to be built up, strengthened and reconstructed through the trans-Newfoundland corridor, which is vital to economic development.
Because of Newfoundland's isolation, the cost of living has increased rapidly. Newfoundland suffers more than any part of Canada because of isolation and the high cost of transportation. Hon. members might be surprised if I mention that Newfoundland has an agricultural base. It can produce almost everything required agriculturally and thus avoid transportation costs. I do not understand the policies of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) with respect to the creation of storage facilities in order to lower the cost of transportation and storage of grain.
In regard to the subsidies which are provided by the Department of Agriculture for vegetable storage facilities, in Newfoundland last year there were two applications. Newfoundland can produce almost anything it requires, such as vegetables, beef, poultry, eggs, milk and other food commodities which are imported at greater cost to the consumer. We must have the support of subsidies and the provision of storage facilities. I hope the minister realizes that potential will help Newfoundland.
The Newfoundland Federation of Agriculture produced figures on laying mash to indicate the price spread among the various provinces. The cost per ton in Quebec was $165, in Nova Scotia it was $172 and in Newfoundland it was $187. That is a difference of approximately 15 per cent. Is it any wonder Newfoundland has the highest cost of living? Because of the additional cost of feed, it is necessary to add one cent to the price of a dozen of eggs.
Newfoundland is the customer of every province west of it. In 1974 the total manufactured shipments from Newfoundland to Canadian destinations were $270 million, while imports totalled approximately $740 million. Newfoundland is shipping too much of its products in their raw state, such as iron ore, unprocessed codfish and pulpwood. There is a trade surplus in the paper industry. The deficits in trade for 1977 in Nova Scotia were $68 million; in New Brunswick, $30 million; and in Quebec, $124 million. Newfoundland requires a comprehensive program to develop its resources for the benefit of its people and Canada.

February 16, 1978

Speaking about the pulp and paper industry, it is in a desperate situation in Newfoundland. Although this is a successful operation, it is threatened by the budworm blight. Unfortunately, because of our distance from markets, the great pulp and paper mills in Newfoundland have difficulties competing. Our exports to the United States which amounted to 80 per cent of our production have decreased to 60 per cent. This is problem which again reflects our need for assistance in transportation.
With respect to the spruce budworm infestation, I had the opportunity, together with some of my colleagues, to meet experts from the Department of the Environment through the auspices of the minister, and we learned from them that the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have reduced the blight through defoliation measures and that only in Newfoundland the infested area has increased last year from three million acres to 3.3 million acres. I know the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand) is trying, with the help of the U.S. government, to increase research in that area to find means of fighting the budworm and at the same time recognize the environmental effects which might result. I hope that we will see the results soon, but this work must be given priority because if we lose our pulp and paper industry in Newfoundland, an industry which is threatened now, I do not know what our future will be.
However, there is still much potential in Newfoundland, and I must commend the minister for providing millions of dollars to various sectors of our economy. We talk about our visions in the north. In Labrador and in northern Newfoundland we have a great potential and we must direct our efforts toward developing it. Experts say that in Labrador there are substantial uranium reserves, but the most realistic potential we have is the hydro potential on Gull Island on the Churchill River in Labrador, a source of renewable energy of which we must take advantage, and the quicker the better. I hope that the minister, together with his colleagues, will recognize the fact that with that energy resource we will be able to provide energy to the people of Newfoundland at a realistic price, and at the same time help the Atlantic provinces as well as develop other industries in northern Newfoundland and Labrador.
As I indicated previously, one of our military lessons was to support the weakest troops. If the government wants ideas about producing jobs, let me point to a housing program which, as I have mentioned many times, is so necessary in Newfoundland, a program called residential rehabilitation assistance. It is recognized that in Newfoundland there are
31,000	homes needing insulation, yet CHIP is directed at the wrong people. It does not assist those who need it most, namely, Newfoundlanders who own their own homes, people with less than $6,000 income and people who cannot afford insulation. There is a program right now which would produce one job in every home which needs repairs. Again I say to the minister that the program should be redirected to assist those people who need it most.

What amazes me is that whenever I ask for money to be allocated to the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program, the minister tells me there is not enough money; yet the government can turn around and provide $1.4 million for the home insulation program, and the people who need it most cannot take advantage of it. I suggest to the minister that we can produce jobs in the way I indicated and that this is a realistic way of providing employment and helping people to insulate their homes at the same time. Again I say there are
31.000	homes in Newfoundland needing insulation, and for every such home there is a job. This would produce at least
31.000	jobs.

They were given a grant of $400,000, but there was a loan factor of $400,000 attached to it so they had to give it up. I must say I am a little amazed at the virulent attacks which the opposition has launched at that conference and at the participants at that conference, particularly in view of the fact that five of the premiers attending the conference are adherents of the Tory doctrine and one is an adherent of the NDP doctrine, although one would never think that members of the NDP here in the House belong to the same party as the premier of Saskatchewan.

tant to note that in the New Brunswick legislature there are 58 representatives of the people, whereas in the federal parliament there are only ten, so each member of the federal parliament from that province represents a much large area and a much larger population.

While I applaud the remarks of the premier of New Brunswick which he made at the first ministers' conference concerning the value of DREE, I wish he would tell the ministers of his government to keep their grubby little paws off federal money and stop using it for patronage and for helping out their political friends.

I hear the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) piping up. If he has any doubt about what I say, I suggest he look at the monstrosity the Conservative government of New Brunswick has built on the Houlton road in New Brunswick. That tourist reception area cost the taxpayers of Canada and New Brunswick almost $3 million. If anyone can justify that, bearing in mind that we need jobs in New Brunswick, I would be glad to listen.
During the sixties real attempts were made by that great New Brunswick premier, the Hon. Louis Robichaud, to bring to the province equality of opportunity for all people of all sectors. Unfortunately, that thrust has been lost. Some areas of the province are now being developed, but little or no attention is being given to other areas.
Two areas of my province are not covered by subsidiary agreements between the federal government and the province. I want to speak about the northwest part of New Brunswick, which is made up principally of Madawaska and Victoria counties, and the area which I represent, commonly known as the Miramichi.
On the Miramichi there is a very high rate of unemployment. We have had great difficulty with our economy for a long time. That has been particularly pronounced in recent years because of weak markets for the primary resources upon which most of us rely for our livelihoods. Very little is being done to enhance the economy of that region or of the northwest region. I understand that DREE is quite prepared to enter into a joint agreement for the development of those regions of the province which are not covered by existing DREE grants, but we cannot get any movement from the provincial government.
I think it is fair to ask why. If DREE is prepared to put money into those areas of the province, what is holding the province back, and how can the federal government work out a comprehensive development strategy for the province of New Brunswick as suggested by this motion? I submit that the federal government cannot act on its own, although it has shown a continuing willingness to do so.
During the period between April, 1966, and the end of March, 1977, total DREE expenditures in New Brunswick
February 16, 1978

amounted to $426.5 million. There are many agreements covered by that amount. Under special area agreements and highways agreements substantial investments have been made in roads, water and sewer and industrial land infrastructure in the Moncton and Saint John special areas. Other efforts have been made to improve the highway network in New Brunswick, but again it is interesting to note that a great deal of money has gone into areas which are already fairly well developed. The Saint John and Moncton areas were undoubtedly in need of a strengthening of their infrastructures to provide broader industrial bases for their citizens, and no one, including me, wishes to take anything away from any other part of the province. What I wonder is why other areas of the province cannot share in the largesse of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion through properly negotiated agreements to give those areas the strengthening they require in order to bring about their own industrial development.
There was the growth centre concept, for instance, and I think it is fair to say that for the entire province the growth centre concept was a failure. There is no doubt that the growth centre concept created some jobs, but the bad side effects outweighed the good effects the concept created. It weakened areas outside the growth centre. Their opportunity to attract industry diminished. Their ability to maintain the industry they had diminished. The growth centre concept caused the reduction of population in some areas. I do not believe that is good policy, so I am glad that it is not being taken very seriously any more.
The FRED agreement resulted in the pumping of millions of dollars into the northeast part of the province of New Brunswick. There have been some spectacular results there as well. The improvement in housing and support facilities for housing development is quite phenomenal. None of this would have been possible or brought to fruition without the assistance of DREE. In the southeast part of New Brunswick we have what is commonly referred to as the southeast agreement which, while not massive in its funding, has been a very worthwhile effort in strengthening the basic infrastructure required for the development of communities and tor attracting industry. Unfortunately, those programs have not covered the area between the northeast and southeast known as the Miramichi except for two little sections on either side.
