speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened to the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) it reminded me of my former profession and I thought that he was perhaps preaching for a call. Certainly with such fervour and emotion he might be welcome in the seriously depleted ranks of the Liberal party in New Brunswick at the present time.
I want to recognize at the outset not only the contribution made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield) when he led off in this important debate but the contribution he has made throughout his career in trying to reverse a very serious trend that has affected the eastern provinces of this country almost since the moment of confederation.
I think the hon. member for Halifax, a former premier of Nova Scotia and former national leader of this party, is one individual who has gained respect on all sides of this House and throughout the country for attempting to tackle very directly the problems confronting a significant proportion of the population of this country.
The motion before us today refers to the need for a com-prenhensive development strategy for the five eastern provinces. 1 think that is the crux of what we are faced with in this debate. Hon. members may have wondered whether the motion was just a series of words without particular meaning or whether it held some special implications for us as federal legislators.
It is important to recognize that the project of trying to deal with regional disparities is relatively new in this country. It is
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
true that since the 1920s there have been attempts to deal in sporadic or specific ways with economic and social disparity. I think it is fair to say that it was not until the time of the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) that there was any conscious attempt to deal with economic disparities.
I would like to give two or three examples to point that up very clearly. There was the development of the ARDA program, the Atlantic adjustment grants, and the Atlantic Development Board. Those three instruments recognized that it was not enough just to have a piecemeal response or an occasional subsidy to deal with one element of disparity or economic difficulty. They recognized that a more comprehensive and consistent approach was required to get at the underlying causes of these economic difficulties.
As I said at the outset, Mr. Speaker, since confederation economic development in Atlantic Canada has lagged behind the Canadian norm by almost any indicator of economic progress. Recent development efforts since the early 1960s have succeeded to some degree in narrowing the income gap. I might say that this has been built chiefly by very large amounts of economic transfers.
In 1976 the following are the transfers made to the Atlantic region: $550 million for unemployment insurance benefits; $208 million in family allowance benefits; $461 million in old age security benefits and $89 million for the Canada pension plan, the largest amount in terms of equalization grants of well over $800 million. These figures together total something in excess of $2.1 billion.
In that same period when we were transferring, by one means or another, a very substantial portion of basic income to the two million residents of Atlantic Canada, we were spending in direct incentives under the Regional Development Incentives Act something like $23 million. We have heard it expressed during recent days by some of the premiers of the eastern provinces speaking at the federal-provincial conference, that Atlantic Canadians and Quebecois are becoming increasingly worried that we are being classed only as consumers and not as producers. That is not a situation this country should accept.
I believe that our region is increasingly in danger of being trapped in its dependency on the federal government for public services, income transfers and even jobs. I am glad that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is here this evening. He is the minister responsible for the very large scale program of Canada Works. I am disturbed at the number of representations I have received from people in my constituency. As the minister well knows, it is one of the areas in the country which has very high unemployment. By varying statistics it is between 15 per cent and 30 per cent.
I am concerned that we have fallen into this continuing round of making funds available for short-term job creation which provides no permanent economic benefit to the region. It provides no opportunity to strengthen and expand the employment possibilities in the basic industries or sectors of
February 16, 1978

the economy, not agriculture, fisheries, tourism or any of the services that support the over-all structure of the economy.
It is more disturbing when you realize that the minister has received representations. I know he has had representations directly from the chairman of my ministerial advisory group saying that if we are to receive these millions of dollars for job creation, then let us make sure the funds that are being expended are not going to create some kind of short-term enthusiasm or interest or opportunity, or long-term frustration and dependency.
I am sorry to say that this government and the minister, while having inaugurated this program some years ago now, are no closer to recognizing that reality as well as the growing economic and social dependency, and the cost included in it, across the country but particularly in the area of eastern Canada which has the highest continuing unemployment. It is too much to expect that the minister would say anything this evening, but I would hope that he would recognize that it is unacceptable to deal with people only in terms of making sure that they have some form of income to continue as consumers, dependent if you like, on the federal handout. It is to reverse that situation that we have this motion before us today.
There must be a development strategy that takes into account both the problems and the potential in the area of transportation, energy, primary resources and the industrial and service sector. Just to look for a moment at the energy question, I was interested in the remarks of the Minister for Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) who correctly said that energy costs in Prince Edward Island are among the highest in the country. If I look at the report which was produced some months ago comparing the average annual energy expense in Canada in a number of cities-these figures were for about a year ago and they would have escalated somewhat in the meantime-I find the figure of $305 for heating in Toronto, $80 for hot water, oil or gas, and $140 for electricity. Compare those costs to costs in Charlottetown, which are $410 for heating, $90 for hot water and $480 for electricity, making the over-all figure for a Prince Edward Island urban resident $980 as compared with a Toronto figure of $525. Lower figures would have been reported for cities in western Canada and slightly higher figures would be reported for other cities in eastern Canada.
This is one indication of disparity alone, Mr. Speaker, where consumers in my province must pay energy rates in some instances almost twice that of their counterparts who live in other urban centres in central and western Canada. It is not enough to make sure that we have some level of unemployment insurance as maintenance income, or family allowance, or Canada Pension Plan benefits, or even employment under Canada Works. If we are not prepared to deal with some of the underlying causes of this growing disparity throughout the years as a result of the energy crisis, we are not going to eliminate regional disparity.
Quite frankly, I think the government has not been willing to recognize that it cannot solve these problems on its own with ad hoc programs. They cannot simply toss in RDIA here,
Regional Disparities
or Canada Works there, or an announcement by the previous minister of finance with respect to some special tax rate, unless all of these are included in some kind of comprehensive approach.
Those of us who come from Prince Edward Island, such as the Minister of Veterans Affairs of the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood), can say something about comprehensive planning. We have seen one aspect of it since 1969 with the Prince Edward Island comprehensive development plan. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, if one was to gauge one's reaction to comprehensive planning only from that experience, one would have to opt in some instances for anarchy rather than for order and planning.
While the Minister of Veterans Affairs waxes eloquently about the great things that have happened under DREE, with the consolidation of the school system, the rapid change in the educational system in Prince Edward Island, I know the hon. member for Malpeque and myself as well as many others would want to add words of caution as to the enormous difficulties that have been created in rural communities and in the educational system itself in trying very quickly to adopt unilaterally an educational system and model which made very little sense for the present or future social and educational needs for the people of Prince Edward Island.
Of course, the comprehensive development plan was a classic example of unilateral intervention by the government. One of the great things about the modern era is that if anyone wishes to check out what really happened with respect to the P.E.I. comprehensive development plan they can see it all on film. The National Film Board has provided an actual record of the process of negotiations that led to the signing of the P.E.I. plan. It underscored the way in which provincial priorities and imperatives were constantly battled and set aside by a federal bureaucracy that had almost no imagination and less sensitivity to the needs of the people living in Prince Edward Island. Talking about the Prince Edward Island development plan is like talking about history, and despite the remarks by the Minister of Veterans Affairs about a second phase, Finding that second phase is like finding the Peking man. We know that it existed once but somehow was lost in the course of a voyage, never to be heard from again. There really is no plan as such today. What does exist, however, are bits and pieces of programs that are the holdovers from the years of the P.E.I. development plan.
What was the reason the plan, which at the outset seemed like a marvellous idea in its basic terms, in terms of development to achieve social and economic goals, seemed to fall so short of success? When it comes right down to the basic reason, it is that the federal government to a large degree, and the provincial government to a lesser degree, did not have faith in the people themselves in terms of their own judgment and participation.
It is now a point of considerable analysis for sociologists and others. However, one aspect of the plan that could have made
2950

February 16, 1978
Regional Disparities
it work, both in its formative stages and in terms of its implementation, was the opportunity for real public participation. Unfortunately, as anyone from Prince Edward Island knows, there was no participation in the formation of the plan. In fact, we played a game of "blind man's buff' during 1968 and 1969 trying to decide what was actually going to be done.
During the months preceding the unveiling of the first phase of the plan, there were leaked portions of the plan that would more or less titillate public opinion on the island to let them in on what would actually happen when the great government decided what their plan would be all about. When it was unveiled, it said a great deal. Unfortunately, however, it was not a plan which the people themselves had an opportunity to formulate and feel they were part of.
Between the years 1969 and 1972 or 1973 there was participation, chiefly through the agency of the rural development council. Even that agency, which basically had been a voluntary association, felt it was a kind of divided house. On the one hand, they felt they had some role to play in terms of community development because that was their basic mandate. On the other hand, they were receiving considerable funds provincially and federally and therefore felt almost in a public relations job for the development plan. That made life extremely difficult for the staff and officers of the rural development council. Of course, even the RDC was able in some way to effectuate public participation, so much so that when the second phase was on the eve of being signed, the provincial government acted quickly to cut off any further funding.
Now, of course, such a thing as public participation being an integral part of the second phase of the plan is simply a non-existent factor. This means if people are not consulted at every stage of the planning and are not involved in preparing for, and participating in, their own future, that which is imposed upon them will obviously be of very superficial duration and effect.
We have profound problems in the Atlantic region. I noticed an article in the local paper the other day regarding a meeting with the Maritime Farmers Council. Dr. Gordon MacEachern, president of the Canadian Agricultural Economics Research Council, a very distinguished former Prince Edward Islander, uttered very sad words of warning. Quoting from a Canadian Development Association prediction he said, and I quote:
-the Atlantic region will lose 50 per cent of its farmers over the next six to seven years and 80 per cent within about 20 years.
He said there were about 10,000 farmers in Nova Scotia in 1966 but there now are only 5,400. By year 2000 the number would shrink to 1,600.
Nowhere had there been more land taken out of agricultural production in the last 20 years than in the maritimes,-
That is an incredible statement when you think how important agriculture is to the economy and the society of the maritime region. He went on to say:
In New Brunswick, farmland was down 52 per cent in the 20-year period, in Nova Scotia 42 per cent and in Prince Edward Island 22 per cent.
That kind of statistical analysis tells us, especially with growing food needs in our country and in the world, that we

must reverse the trend. We must not simply subsidize and basically create efficient units in agriculture. We must turn the agricultural industry into a dynamic, important development component of the Atlantic region. It can and must be done. However, given the direction and the trend of this government's performance, one cannot be greatly encouraged.
In the area of transportation, the hon. member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) has repeatedly reminded the Minister of Transport and members of this House that we cannot have any kind of overall development strategy unless transportation plays a constructive and useful role.
1 know the minister who is here this evening would echo those words very strongly. He knows that his principal problem in some ways is not the effective administration of his own department but trying to get a useful measure of co-operation and co-ordination from other key departments, whether it be transport, finance, energy, or any other departmental policies which have an impact upon the five eastern provinces.
The sad fact is that when this department was established under the minister's predecessor in 1969, hundreds and thousands of words were echoed in this place and in committee about the importance of this new ministry which would, in effect, be a kind of super ministry. It was going to ensure there was a co-ordinated, effective, over-all development strategy. What has happened? All we have now is the minister trying to achieve some kind of bilateral agreement with each of the provinces in turn, trying to shore up an RDIA program that seems increasingly irrelevant to the process of the development of the Atlantic region, Quebec and elsewhere.
What we need is a refreshed mandate that will be committed to a comprehensive program of development. If this debate achieves nothing else, I hope it will remind this minister and the government that they have a major role to play, at least as major as it is possible to play given their performance to date, or until they can be succeeded by a government that will surely do it!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I was surprised by that sudden interest and astonishing fondness shown by the Progressive Conservative party for Quebec, especially for eastern Quebec. However, 1 am not so surprised when 1 consider and realize that the sponsor of the motion is not the Progressive Conservative party, but the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield). Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax is, in my opinion, the only former leader of the Progressive Conservative party who has tried to learn and understand Quebec and its inhabitants.
If I could be allowed to make a suggestion-which evidently will not be followed-to the present Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) and his supporters, it would be to listen carefully, as he did during his speech, to the hon. member for Halifax and act upon his advice on Quebec, because I think he is the best adviser the Progressive Conservative party and
February 16, 1978

more especially the Leader of the Opposition could have at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, after this short departure from the subject, I want to say that I am glad of the opportunity given to me by the hon. member for Halifax to talk about regional economic expansion, the expansion of regions where economic progress is slower than elsewhere in the country, my region among others.
None of the legislation put forward by the various governments, be they federal or provincial, none of the measures they have taken has given perfect results; perfection, as we all know, is not of this world. But, Mr. Speaker, no one can deny that the act of 1969 creating the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has resulted in benefits and important advantages for the communities it was meant to help. So it was to be expected that this legislaon would come up against certain obstacles which would prevent it from reaching its objective-improving the economy of those regions where economic growth was long overdue and did not allow the people to find the proper means to pull themselves up to the same level as other parts of the country.
Besides being isolated from large centres, one of the obstacles which preclude economic growth in some parts of our country is that industry itself, well set up in large centres with all their opportunities as a marketplace and so on, was not naturally attracted by our designated areas. Yet, in spite of this, regions such as Montreal and Quebec city were designated later in an attempt to decentralize towards peripheral areas.
Mr. Speaker, we have no doubt whatsoever about the beneficial effects generated in our regions with the creation of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. When I first came to the House in 1962, at the same time as Your Honour, I was concerned over the lower economic conditions of the area which I have always represented and maybe because of the negligence of preceding governments, our region was in an underdeveloped state and did not benefit from programs available to the rest of Canada.
That is why we had insisted during the campaign on the fact that under a Liberal administration, financial assistance would contribute to the economic development of areas such as ours-and I know there are a great many other such regions in Canada and especially in the Atlantic provinces-and provide our people with decent living conditions.
So it is that following our assuming power in 1963, we adopted for instance the industry incentive policy, which encouraged corporations to establish their operations in areas such as ours. As early as 1963 or 1964, a corporation came to my riding to develop very significantly the forest industry. Without the incentives provided by the then Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, this industry would never have started its operation in the Gaspe area. That was only the beginning, and later, in 1969, we witnessed the creation of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and the first incumbent of this portfolio unless I am mistaken, the Hon.
Regional Disparities
Jean Marchand, now a senator, then a very distinguished hon. member from the province of Newfoundland, and now benefits from the efficiency of the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Lessard), the present minister of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion whom, leaving aside all political considerations, I want to congratulate for his interest in regional development and all he had done to date under difficult circumstances to help the development and economic progress of my province.
Not so long ago I was very unhappy to hear that the abolition of DREE was being considered, just as I do not like to hear the opposition say it has served no good purpose, that regional disparities still exist and that the department has done nothing. Well, it is easy to say nothing has been done, but taking the province of Quebec, I have given a few examples in my riding of subsidies to industry. Taking them by area, the Gaspe Peninsula, the St. Lawrence River and the lower St. Lawrence-of course, one always starts with an area close to one's heart-well, where subsidies to industry are concerned the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, therefore the federal government-which is being blamed lately of doing nothing, and again not long ago, a few days ago as a matter of fact here in Ottawa, through the premier of Quebec-has made quite a few grants. As of December 31, 1977, the Gaspe Peninsula and the lower St. Lawrence received grants from the federal Department of Regional Economic Expansion in the amount of $10,849,717; the Saguenay and Lac-Saint-Jean area, $14,000,942; the Quebec city area, $44,116,150; the Trois-Rivieres region, $65,381,078; the eastern Townships, $16,604,976; Montreal, $87,707,848; the Ottawa Valley region, $2,713,989; northwestern Quebec, $30,446,784; the north shore, $20,593,354, for a total of $292,414,838; which would make on an acceptable investment of $1,501,446,952 for a total job production of $72,507.
The FODER agreement, which deals mainly with the problems of the Gaspe Peninsula and the lower St. Lawrence, had invested, as of October 7, 1977, $148,575,576 in agriculture, forests, fishing, mining, leasure, tourism, business, urban planning, transportation, social development, administration and participation in forest redevelopment, under an ancillary agreement, revised and signed June 22, 1977, an estimated $3,950,000, $2,370,000 being from the federal government, in land treatment, including drainage, $4,750,000, including $3,000,000 from the federal government.
So it cannot be said, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has not done anything for regional disparities. As for the lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe Peninsula, it is only since the creation of the department, since certain incentives are given to companies for settling there that we have known renewed growth in economic activities. In the field of transportation, for example, we have established a roll-on roll-off ferry system, which has developed the tourist industry in the Magdalen Islands, whose only industry was fishing. Today, the islands enjoy a fairly good revenue from tourism, due to this ferry which is part of the regional economic development program.

I would like to come back to the question of air transport about which everyone has been talking for a long time. For my part, I have been talking about it for ten years in relation with the Magdalen Islands. It is the only means of transport available from December until April in the Magdalen Islands.
I have been requesting improvements to the airport since 1968; some improvements have been made, but they still do not meet the needs of the population for adequate transportation. At the present time, the Magdalen Islands cannot be assured of regular service because we do not have the necessary equipment, that is instrument flights, since the present runways and the many hills prevent installation of proper instruments. We have been asking for improvements for ten years and nothing has been done. Numerous studies have been made. The Eastern Quebec Planning Bureau has made certain studies and we have of course kept the Magdalen Islands airport in mind, but we have still not received an answer.
Today I had the pleasure-and for this I would like to credit the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang)-to hear that a private firm, which says that its experts know everything about the socioeconomic conditions of our area, has been commissioned to study the best location for a regional airport in the Gaspe area-SOme will say that it is just another study, but this one will be made by an independent firm and not the Department of Transport. Some may wonder what this has to do with the Magdalen Islands, but it has a lot to do with the islands since the company now providing service from the province of Quebec to the Magdalen Islands would like to develop the airport at Havre-aux-Maisons in the Magdalen Islands, but this can not be done before a regional airport is built or the Gaspe airport is improved.
This is why we applaud the decison made by the department, following repeated requests on our part, to commission an independent firm to study the most economically and sociologically suited location for this airport within three months. Transport is a major factor of economic development. In this regard, I must thank the Department of Regional Economic Expansion for listening to our complaints and finally accepting to assist in the construction of a road to the Gaspe area. We are satisfied with what has been spent through its financial participation with the province of Quebec to the construction of this road which, we hope, will soon be completed. We are satisfied with this participation but we will be even more satisfied when Gaspe will be able to have an air transportation system meeting its needs for 1978 as well as its future needs, as far as economic development is concerned.
A salt mine has been discovered in the Magdalen Islands. Several of my colleagues in the House have asked me questions after the release of reports in the press and on the radio, people who seem to be against the development of this salt mine. Those who are opposed to it are people from outside who went to the Magdalen Islands to try to convince people that from an environmental and aesthetic point of view the development of a mine in the Magdalen Islands could be detrimental to the tourists who would visit the islands.
(Mr. Bdchard.]
Tourism is a part of our economy and lasts two or three months of the year, but Magdalen Islands residents have to earn a living all year long. So the question is: Are the people from the islands opposed to the development of the salt mine? No, they are not. The opposition coming from the Magdalen Islands originates from a group of fishermen who are rightly wondering about the site which will be chosen as the harbour used to get the salt off the islands. It might have harmful effects on the lobster grounds, as I mentioned some time ago when I asked a question to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) and to which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave me an answer.
I am therefore asking for a serious study to be undertaken, but I want to stress the fact that the people from the Magdalen Islands are not opposed to the development of that mine. On the contrary, it will represent a welcome boost to the economy of the islanders, given the present state of fisheries which is getting somewhat better. Such a development could allow a good many people from the Magdalen Islands to earn a living all year round and expect a sizeable income, not to mention other side effects that it may bring about.
The development of that mine depends on another important project in the continental Bonaventure riding which would create from two to three thousand new jobs in the area of Port Daniel. This is why I am making a request tonight to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion while paying homage to him for the magnificent job he is doing for the country and for his province. That reminds me of the premier from that province who was complaining this week of the lack of consideration his province is getting, in his opinion-we saw that Premier slam the door, but any other attitude on the part of Mr. Levesque would have been surprising for when he comes to Ottawa, it is to laugh at people. He comes to laugh at the federal government because he has made up his mind, he has been a separatist since the November 15, 1976, election. He already considers Quebec as a separate state, so why should he not slam the doors? He comes here to make an act of presence and then drowses off, as it has been reported in some newspapers.
My request then to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is for him to continue his efforts in favour of the economic development of our province as he has done up to now and I am asking him to answer positively any requests that the government of Quebec might submit to him and particularly with regard to the issue in which I am interested, namely the assistance required for the development of the salt mine and any other industry which will come in addition to the development of that mine in the riding of Bonaventure, at Port Daniel.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is plain to be seen that the hon. gentleman from Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) has learned some of the courtesies of this House, unlike the hon. member for North-
February 16, 1978

umberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne). I compliment the hon, member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine for his constructive and positive remarks on behalf of his constituency.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that the $100 million mentioned by the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi came from two sources: Fifty per cent came from the provincial treasuries and 50 per cent from that which was not to be paid out from the federal treasury in the subsidies to be sacrificed by the maritime treasuries, specifically transportation subsidies. Therefore, the $100 million does not cost the federal treasury one farthing in the long run, and that is not much to brag about, sir.
Secondly, that hon. member remembered that there was a premier by the name of Robichaud in the province of New Brunswick, and well he should, and as I do. But what he did not say or would not acknowledge was that when Mr. Hatfield became the premier of New Brunswick, the deal then in existence with the outgoing premier was no longer applicable to the province of New Brunswick and had to be renegotiated on terms imposed by Ottawa different from those which had been conceded to a Liberal premier, namely, Premier Robichaud. That does not make it sound very much like what the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi said, and that is why I was perhaps a little rude to you, Mr. Speaker, in trying to correct the record.
I want to be constructive in respect of the Atlantic area. Unlike the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi, I am interested in its wellbeing and its promotion. I am not interested in petty politics. I am interested in the things which can make the area great and become self-sustaining, and this can be done.
The area is rich in renewable resources and is primarily dependent upon them; that is, forestry, fishing and agriculture. The fishing industry under the direction of successive ministers in Ottawa has had its assets traded away in international agreements with no known return to any part of Canada in any way, shape or form. This resource was depleted in the reckless dealing which took place. We did not impose the 200-mile limit even as early as Iceland, and by the time we did it was almost a matter of locking the door after the horse was literally and completely stolen. There have been steps taken to try to reconstruct this in an eleventh hour repentance, I might add. There are a few things which I think can still be done.
We are losing a generation of fishermen by virtue of regulations in respect of licensing which have been imposed by the government of Canada. On behalf of the Atlantic area, I plead with this government to do one of two things; either restore the licensing privilege to inshore fishermen so that the sons of the present fishermen may also fish, or assess the impact of the renewal of these licences on the species of stock, and explain why they cannot do so.
Even though the catch of the handliner and other inshore fishermen is minuscule, because of the present price of fish this catch is important as a source of income for tens of hundreds
Regional Disparities
of Atlantic fishermen. It is important to restore the licensing fee, or measure the impact upon the stock and justify the restrictions which are presently in place. Perhaps some will not be liberalized, perhaps others can be. In any case, any relief would be helpful. I have proposed this on several occasions. I have asked for an official estimate of the impact, but I have received no answer.
The employment and income possibilities which the fishing industry presents is well worthy of federal investment. Though this is a time of austerity, it is not the time for austerity in investment. There is a difference. Investment in an industry with the potential of the fishing industry will furnish dividends to all Canadians. I am proposing more expenditure of the investment type. Failure to invest will express economic ignorance of the fishing fact. Boats, wharves and processing plants are becoming outmoded. All of these things require federal assistance for replacement. Neglect over the years has put the fishing industry in a dependent position. It can recover and pay dividends to Canada.
This applies as well to the fields of agriculture. Because of time constraints, I have to be extremely brief. In the field of agriculture, the Atlantic area is not self-sufficient in many of the products it is capable of producing. It is not self-sufficient in meat, butter, poultry products and grains. Perhaps it is a little over self-sufficient in the production of potatoes and apples.
The maritime provinces need research. One of the threats the department has held over agriculture in the Atlantic area is the withdrawal of freight rate subsidies on cereal grains. This subsidy goes on only from budget to budget. It cannot be withdrawn unless the livestock and poultry industries in Atlantic Canada fall dead, or until such time as there are alternative grains to grow on a viable basis. To date those grains have not been discovered.
I have pleaded with agriculture to try varieties from foreign sources, because the native varieties are not viable on the east coast. This is not being done. I have pleaded for research in the agricultural industry with respect to potatoes, grain, etc. This research could determine what the climate of the Atlantic provinces had to offer, and what would be required in engineering, farm buildings, farm storage, animal husbandry in the barns, poultry houses and hog pens. What may be applicable in Idaho, Maine or New York State does not necessarily lend itself to the climate of the Atlantic area. We require research into the storing of potatoes and the proper housing of livestock.
It is to this field that the Department of Agriculture and the government of Canada have not directed any attention. Research can help to make the Atlantic agricultural industry self-supporting. It requires leadership and investment. We cannot continue with the uncertainties of a budget to budget subsidy for feed and cereal grains, and at the same time fail to expand the research structure which is necessary. We must explore the world for varieties to find those which will grow viably in our country.
Forestry is perhaps the most important of all our renewable resources. Historically it has been plagued by fire, parasites

February 16, 1978
Regional Disparities
and disease. Added to this in the last few years has been the economic impact of inflation, the high cost of money, high capital costs and increasing labour costs. No single one of the economic forces is totally to blame, but the industry finds itself in a position where it is difficult to compete in the international markets which are necessary for its prosperity.
For some 25 years the spruce and fir forests have been plagued by budworms. Initially the federal government recognized that it was a specific and isolated program which deserved support. It assisted financially for a short period of time, but research for an alternative was not commenced. That is the key: research to determine the specifics of prosperity in renewable resources. The province of New Brunswick was left to take all the environmental criticism aimed at it for spraying the budworm. The government had pictures in its files that it did not bother to show. Those were pictures of test plots which were not sprayed. As a result of that, there is not a live spill on a coniferous tree in those areas. Therefore, if spraying had not occurred, New Brunswick would have been as fiery red as the deadest tree.
The government did not indicate that there was no known way to control budworm other than by insecticide. The only ways it has evern been controlled is when the budworm eats itself out of house and home and starves to death, or is consumed by the fire which follows the devastation. But the government did not bother to inform the public of those facts. That is not fair to the Atlantic region. That area requires the support of the federal government in this regard.
The government has very gently, and not very effectively, advertised some of Canada's natural attractions. The hospitality of people in Atlantic Canada is unexcelled. Atlantic Canada is where the history of Canada was started. Canada was developed from east to west. Settlers arrived on the east coast for various reasons. Some were starved out of Ireland during the potato famine, some arrived as Quakers because they were unable to practise their religion in their native land.
There is an historic Indian campsite and battleground at Fort Meductic. There is adequate material available to establish a small museum there. Can the island where Champlain spent his first winter be found on a map depicting Canadian historic sites of interest? I do not think so. It is not on the map. The government has done a poor promotional job. If the government developed and expanded Canadian historic sites as part of its make work projects, thousands of tourists would be attracted to the Atlantic area. The opportunity is present. Does Canada want to fulfil its responsibility for developing these sites for the tourist industry?
Two things are necessary for income to be derived from renewable resources. First, there must be a fair trade policy. We cannot accept the position of the Tariff Board when it reported that it would reduce tariffs on potatoes and potato processed products imported into Canada to a level roughly equal to the tariff levied on the same products exported to the United States. Atlantic Canada requires a fair trade policy if agriculture, fisheries and forestry are to survive.

Second, we cannot accept the ever increasing rate of freight rates on products going out. This is particularly unacceptable when we find that the forest industry today is trucking its product from mills in New Brunswick across the border of the state of Maine, putting it on American railroads and shipping it at their freight rates at a saving to the industry. We must be competitive in U.S. markets, and when the freight rate is so far out of line that all goods must go across the CNR and the CPR over into Maine to be loaded on American lines, there is something wrong with our transportation policy.
The other day the minister laid the blame on the MacPher-son report. MacPherson put in a report years ago, but today the minister is responsible for policy and for freight rates, air traffic rates, ocean rates and ferry rates in Canada. That is his baby. But, like the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) and all other ministers, he accepts no responsibility but rather finds a head on which to lay the blame.
We need positive action, as an investment in Atlantic Canada, in creating competitive and fair freight rates. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went into the first ministers' conference without a single positive recommendation on what could be done for any part of Canada. I suggest that we should adjust our freight rates to a fair and competitive rate, have a policy of free trade, make an investment in our Atlantic ports, invest in our shipyards, and adjust our policy in respect of the export of energy, particularly as it relates to petroleum products. Because every refinery in eastern Canada, from Come-By-Chance to Saint John, New Brunswick, is subject to unfavourable regulations in respect of our exports of refined products, which are an important source of the revenue of virtually all refineries. But the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) has created regulations in respect of the export of any petroleum product from eastern Canada, so that from month to month and from year to year the products are exported on an unpromised renewable basis. We are now considered in the United States as another unreliable foreign source of energy.
I ask that we become a friendly and reliable source of energy so that the Atlantic area becomes a refining centre and a centre of employment and income for all of Canada. That does not exist there today. Let us expand our shipyards, let us get a merchant marine subsidized by the government, let us build our naval ships in Canada and expand our shipyards so that we can do that. I only wish time would permit a further expansion of positive ideas for the government because Atlantic people are proud people and we want the proper policies to make us self-supporting.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT STRATEGIES FOR EASTERN QUEBEC AND ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, being allowed the last five minutes is a dubious honour in this debate, but I would like to participate as a non-maritimer and point out several things which I think should be said. One of them is that many maritime members have spoken today of their individual problems in their individual ridings. Perhaps it
February 16, 1978

is good to have had a mini-throne speech debate-each of the members being first time members they can make that kind of speech-but it does indicate that one problem we have in Canada is having a large disadvantaged area which all Canadians wish to assist and which cannot be assisted by giving everybody everything they want.
For that reason 1 was particularly interested in the contributions of hon. members regarding the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Government members said they appreciated the work which the minister had done, and opposition members said he has not done enough. DREE was set up to assist the disadvantaged regions in our country. Certainly northern Ontario should not have been left out, because although we are part of the richest province in Canada, the wealth has not rubbed off on northern Ontario. We still have many resources, but they have taken our wealth and given us very little in return.
This raises a problem which is quite self-evident. It seems to me the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Les-sard) will have to give consideration to making more effective use of his department and his officials. The many experts in his department should not try to make agreements with the provinces and the regions that satisfy solely the political ambitions of these provinces and regions. Rather the department should have enough scope and brain power to decide how best to spend the money provided in the area and how to make the longest term agreement which will produce the most advantage. Undoubtedly we want to help the maritimes. There is some doubt about Quebec, about whether we want to engage in long term projects there. Many of us want to see what will happen there before we do so, but that is not true of the maritimes.
We have had problems with the maritime provinces ever since they became part of confederation. Some of them may be solved and some may not. Many times they have been victims of what the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) and others have referred to as patronage. When the government changes, the minister must immediately negotiate a new DREE agreement with that province. I say nuts to that. We should spend our Canadian money in the most effective way so as to produce the most jobs.
I should like to point out one other problem which exists not only in the maritimes but also in my area. This afternoon I attended one of the committee meetings and listened to a discussion about Syncrude. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said that Syncrude would not have existed had we not put money into it. If we put money into any DREE project, what excuse do we have for not taking equity in the industry we assist? In the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, or, for instance, in the Ottawa Valley a year or so ago, 50 per cent of the projects in which we put money went bankrupt. What did we do with our share of money which we put into equity? We did nothing with it. If we had had brains in the department we could have said that management was not operating properly. Management does not want to lose money and go
Adjournment Debate
bankrupt, but we could not assist them where assistance was absolutely necessary.
This is true all across the maritimes with regard to projects in which we become involved, such as the steel plant, the heavy water plant and the coal mines. In many cases we must give them more than money, we must give them the assistance of our federal and provincial experts. We should not be scared of acquiring equity. We are doing this in many other fields today where we know we will have to give additional assistance and advice. We have started many projects in the maritimes which have failed. They have failed because of the squabbling of the provincial government, the squabbling of the federal government and the squabbling between one region and another. The national government is big enough to provide assistance, direction and leadership, but all too often federal leadership is non-existent.

subtopic: GRAIN-POSSIBILITY ELEVATOR AT MOOSE JAW ABLE TO SERVICE CHURCHILL-REQUEST FOR STUDY
GRAIN-POSSIBILITY ELEVATOR AT MOOSE JAW ABLE TO SERVICE CHURCHILL-REQUEST FOR STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 30, as recorded at page 2394 of Hansard, I posed a question to the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board asking him whether he was prepared to carry out a feasibility study to determine whether the Canadian government elevator facilities at Moose Jaw could be used to service the port of Churchill. I followed that question with a supplementary question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) asking whether he had discussed with the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board the feasibility of using the drying facilities at the Moose Jaw terminal to dry damp grain from the northern part of our province so that there could be sales for that grain.
Neither minister gave a satisfactory answer to my questions. In the Hall commission report it was recommended that a new government elevator be built at Yorkton. That elevator would be capable of cleaning and storing some 25 million to 30 million bushels of grain per year, which could be shipped to Churchill. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board subsequently appointed one Rod Bryden to do a study on the recommended Yorkton terminal, and although I have not seen the Bryden report, it is my understanding that it recommends against construction of such a terminal.
In view of the fact that the Moose Jaw terminal is only about 150 miles further from Churchill than Yorkton and that

February 16, 1978
Adjournment Debate
the elevator at Moose Jaw is capable of a throughput of some 30 million bushels of grain per annum-and that is grain cleaned to export standards, I might add-it seems to me that the Moose Jaw elevator could be utilized to service the port of Churchill. Unfortunately, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board would not undertake to carry out a feasibility study.
The Moose Jaw terminal has a capacity of about 5.5 million bushels. It has up to date cleaning and drying facilities and is capable of loading enough hopper cars in a 24-hour period to make up sufficient unit trains to load a one million bushel grain ship. Yet in the 17-year period from the fiscal year 1959-60 to the fiscal year 1975-76, car shipments from the terminal at Moose Jaw averaged less than 1,000 or, on the average, shipments of about two million bushels per year. Compare that with a possible throughput of 30 million bushels; approximately 7 per cent of the capacity. What a waste!
The annual reports of the Canadian Wheat Board over three crop years, 1973-74 to 1975-76 inclusive, show that demurrage charges in the three-year period totalled some $19,190,808. Admittedly, some of these charges were incurred as a result of rail strikes, derailments of trains or rock slides in the Fraser Valley, but in many instances they were incurred because the proper grade of grain was not available at the coastal terminals. These demurrage charges are a direct charge to the grain producer.
A ship does not suddenly turn up in a harbour looking for a load of grain. A ship is in transit for many days and sometimes for two or three weeks. Its estimated time of arrival at port must be known many days in advance by the Canadian Wheat Board. The estimated time of arrival would be changed only as a result of storms, which are predictable, and news of any delay would be transmitted by radio. If it is known in advance that a boat is coming and what grade of grain is required, and if the grain is not available in terminal position, why would it not be possible to utilize the facilities of a government inland terminal such as Moose Jaw to place the required grain in export position in a matter of a few days?
The Minister of Agriculture, in response to my supplementary question, states as follows:
We must also keep in mind that there is a private elevator system in the western provinces. This is a government elevator. If the hon. member is suggesting that we put it in direct competition with the private elevator system, he should suggest that and we will bring in an amendment to the bill immediately to allow just that.
While the private grain trade is interested in making its system pay, I am sure that the producer-owned companies are also interested in seeing that their producer members realize as high a price as possible for the grain that they sell. It seems to me that an elevator such as the Moose Jaw terminal, which has a capacity of 5'/2 million bushels, could be filled to capacity and grain shipped when it appeared that there might be a delay at a coastal terminal because of the lack of the proper grade of grain, and that a ship might have to wait in port with the resultant demurrage charges to the producer.

I know the employees of the government elevator in Moose Jaw. The are keen and anxious to work and are frustrated by the lack of utilization of their elevator. It seems a shame to me that the excellent facilities that are available there should be underutilized year by year when there could be a saving to the taxpayer and more money in the hands of the producers if the facilities were properly utilized.
I am sure that if the ministers who responded to my questions would sit down and discuss the use of the Moose Jaw terminal and other inland terminals, as I have suggested, with members of the producer-owned grain companies, some agreement could be arrived at. It is my belief that the officials of these grain companies are sincere and interested in putting as many dollars into the pockets of the western grain producers as is possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Donald Wood (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: GRAIN-POSSIBILITY ELEVATOR AT MOOSE JAW ABLE TO SERVICE CHURCHILL-REQUEST FOR STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, unfortunately the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lapointe) had a previous commitment this evening so I am happy to reply to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil.)
We are continually looking at all the ways in which we can improve the use of the port of Churchill. Before considering the economic feasibility of various proposals for collecting grain on the prairies that is destined for export via Churchill, we must make an assessment of several other matters. We must consider, for example, the relative rail costs of shipping grain to Churchill versus other ports. Maintaining a rail line over permafrost such as the line to Churchill poses difficult problems not experienced elsewhere in our grain handling system.
In our current program of rehabilitating prairie rail lines the federal government has allotted $1,610,000 to the line to Churchill. The work involved includes bank widening and drainage, rail relay and extending the sidings. It is likely that large sums of money will have to be spent on this line just to maintain its current capacity, let alone to increase it.
The government of Canada has also allotted significant sums of money to improving Churchill port facilities. In 1978, $5,575,000 in capital expenditures have been allocated to Churchill. This work includes scale automation and metrication, port lighting, winter berthing facilities, repairs and dredging.
In a period when we have limited amounts of capital to spend on upgrading our handling and transportation system, we must ask where our money will be most profitably spent. When one considers that the port of Vancouver can export as much in one month as Churchill does in a season, it becomes apparent that a careful analysis of the market potential for Churchill must be done before large capital expenditures are committed.
A careful economic assessment of this marketing route will have to be conducted. Although the port is closer to some of our European customers than Thunder Bay, insurance rates are higher while the shipping season is shorter.
February 16, 1978

It must be observed that the present system of primary elevators collecting grain on the prairies for Churchill has performed adequately. The port has approached its practical maximum capacity in each of the last two years. The elevators have done a good job and can be expected to be even more effective in the future as they continue to modernize their facilities. The government can also be expected to construct the necessary facilities to service the future needs of the port of Churchill.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-DENIAL OF PENSIONS TO WIDOWS UNDER AGE 65-GOVERNMENT ACTION
SOCIAL SECURITY-DENIAL OF PENSIONS TO WIDOWS UNDER AGE 65-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question to which I address myself tonight concerns the spouse's allowance for those citizens who are given the opportunity to qualify for the old age pension at the age of 60 if their spouse is 65.
We have discussed regional disparities tonight, and we have discussed the situation regarding the five million poverty stricken Canadians in the country. Thus it is very difficult to understand the direction the government is taking regarding senior citizens who qualify for the pension on reaching the age of 65 years. If a spouse happens to be 60 years of age, he or she also qualifies. God forbid, though, if the spouse who is 65 dies at 66 and the other spouse is 61! Then he or she is completely cut off from the old age pension. Where is the reasoning for this in this supposed prosperous country of ours?
In my province that particular survivor has to revert to welfare. The amount of welfare could vary from $140 to $191 a month, depending on assets owned. However, the average fuel bill for a single family home-and I believe there are around 11,000 single family homes in Newfoundland-is from $60 to $120 a month, depending upon the condition of the home.
Let me read a letter from a senior citizen to give the House an example. This letter is from a lady who is 64 years of age.
I am writing to you with another problem. 1 worked as a gas attendant right up until July, 1976 when I reached the age of 64 years. I filed for my unemployment, but did not receive any moneys until the middle of September. I then sent a form in to St. John's for my spouse's allowance and all I got a month (spouse's allowance) was $36 a month-
Now, Mr. Speaker, here is a person 64 years of age working as a gas attendant in order to earn extra income to provide the basic necessities of life. She was turned down, and I have since learned that she was refused. But this is the situation that exists. It is difficult to understand. I am sure that every member in this House, other than the particular minister responsible, will recognize this is a glaring inequity. I am pleased to collaborate with my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has the same concerns as I about this matter.
Hopefully the very capable hon. member who is to reply will impress upon his caucus, or through other means which are available to him, this extremely serious plight of our pension-
Adjournment Debate
ers. Let me quote some words of Benjamin Disraeli which are apropos to this situation. They appeared in the National Enquirer.
Two nations, between whom there is no intercourse and no sympathy; who are as ignorant of each other's habits, thoughts and feelings as if they were dwellers in different zones, or inhabitants of different planets; who are formed by different breeding, are fed by different food, are ordered by different manners, and are not governed by the same laws-the rich and the poor.
I ask the parliamentary secretary who will reply that some consideration be given to those people who, through no fault of their own, cannot manage with the high cost of living. I hope we can impress upon the government in this session the needs of those who depend on us to help them.

speakeroldname: Mr. Frank Maine (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-DENIAL OF PENSIONS TO WIDOWS UNDER AGE 65-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whereas I am very sympathetic to the problem described by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), I must report that the spouse's allowance was introduced because the government of Canada recognized the plight faced by many older couples trying to manage on only one pension. To help these couples, the government now provides a spouse's allowance to a person 60 to 64 years of age whose spouse is receiving an old age security pension. The amount of this allowance varies according to the other income of the retired couple, and for couples with substantial income, no such allowance is payable.
A spouse's allowance ceases when the pensioner dies. It has been argued that once a spouse qualifies for the spouse's allowance, it should be paid until that spouse qualifies for the old age security pension in his or her own right, to avoid hardship that would arise from terminating the allowance on the death of the pensioner. However, it would be difficult to explain in the case of a pensioner's death why his or her surviving spouse would continue to receive the spouse's allowance, whereas other surviving spouses who never qualified for the allowance are denied it.
The spouse's allowance is also terminated when the spouses separate, is suspended if either or both spouses leave Canada for a period greater than six months, or if either spouse is imprisoned for longer than 90 days. Essentially, the spouse's allowance is paid when the couple are living together on the same income. When these circumstances no longer apply, the allowance is either terminated or suspended.
The spouse's allowance is not available to widowed, single, divorced or separated persons in the 60 or 64 years age range. If the allowance had been made more generally available, this would have, in effect, led to a general reduction of the retirement age in Canada from 65 to 60, and it was not felt that the country could afford such a reduction. Therefore, it was decided that this program should deal with the one specific problem, so that older married couples, with one spouse already on pension, could meet their financial requirements through the old age security program rather than through other programs such as the Canada Assistance Plan.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED PROVISION OF PENSIONS FOR PERSONS IN NEED BETWEEN AGES 60 AND 65
SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED PROVISION OF PENSIONS FOR PERSONS IN NEED BETWEEN AGES 60 AND 65
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if my opening sentence is one of criticism, I should like to make it clear that it is not directed to either of the two parliamentary secretaries who are here tonight. I must point out that in my view the practice is developing, almost to the point of abuse, of ministers not being here to respond to questions on the late show; and too often it is not even the minister's parliamentary secretary but some other parliamentary secretary who is called on to do the job. That is not a criticism of either of the two Liberals who adorn the government benches tonight, but I hope the point will be noted.
My question is in the same area as the one dealt with by my friend, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). It was asked on Monday, November 28, and appears at page 1291 of Hansard for that date. The gist of the question was in these words:
In view of the growing number of persons between 60 and 65 years of age, most of them spinsters and widows, who express utter disbelief that there is an allowance for spouses but nothing for persons of single status, will the minister take the necessary steps to see that an equivalent allowance is made available to all persons between the ages of 60 and 65 who need it, regardless of their marital status?
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) gave me an answer which indicated that she understood the question. However, the best she gave me was an assurance that the whole matter, and even more than that, was being studied.
Like the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, I am not at all satisfied with the answer the parliamentary secretary gave to my hon. friend's question. But I will say for him that he did repeat the basis upon which the spouse's allowance was introduced, as stated at that time by the government. He said the whole philosophy was that the government had realized that two persons could not live on one pension. So the government said that where one spouse was over 65 and the other one was between 60 and 65, it would provide two pensions.
We agreed then, and we agree now, that two persons cannot live on one pension. But we asked then, and we ask now: If the government agrees that two people cannot live on one pension, how does it think one person can live on no pension at all? It is usually women between 60 and 65 who get no pension, because they are in that age bracket and are single or widowed. Yet if they happened to have a husband who was over 65, they would get it.
We still feel that basing the spouse's allowance on the basis of marital status is unfair. The parliamentary secretary is quite right when he says that some of the things we advocate would seem to open the door to lowering the pensionable age to 60. Mr. Speaker, I have been trying to push that door open for some time and I shall keep on trying to do so. But until we reach that point I stress that the present system is grossly unfair, especially to women.
The government talks about this legislation being equal. It is defined as for the spouse. You get it whether you are a female or a male spouse. Nevertheless, in our culture most wives are younger than their husbands, and when we look at the employment picture we find that most of the single persons between 60 and 65 who are getting no allowance are women. Most of those who find their allowance cut off because the older spouse has died are also women. The letter of sympathy which the department sends out is one of those "either/or" documents which apply whether it is sent to a widow or a widower.
I am not pleading tonight for an overall program. I shall do that on another occasion. I want the pensionable age to be brought down to 60, but I am pleading that in the meantime the government should not be so unfair to single women and to widows. People who encounter this legislation for the first time ask me: Is it possible? How could parliament ever have passed a bill which provides for an allowance to the spouse of an older person but not to a woman in the same age bracket who has no spouse?
The parliamentary secretary came up with another argument-and I agree with him-that to continue a payment to the spouse who has been receiving it and who has become a widow raises the question: What about the woman who is a widow over the age of 60 and who never got it? In my view, this underlines the justice of my whole case-that all women in that bracket who need an allowance should get it regardless of their marital status.
The parliamentary secretary is looking at me, saying he knows what 1 think. He is right. I want to see the pension paid at age 60 to all persons out of the labour market. But at this stage I think those who need it between 60 and 65, women in particular, should get it without regard to marital status.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will take this matter up with the minister, who is a woman herself. Surely there is someone over there with the heart and the compassion to deal with this issue.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-SUGGESTED PROVISION OF PENSIONS FOR PERSONS IN NEED BETWEEN AGES 60 AND 65
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure there is the heart and the compassion. There is just not the money.
The hon. member has asked about the possibility of providing a benefit on the same basis as the spouse's allowance to those persons between 60 and 65 years of age who do not qualify for the allowance because they are not the spouse of an old age security pensioner. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has earlier expressed her sympathy and concern for this group of people. As she said, the department is in the process of examining the priorities which must be set when determining where the limited funds available for groups of Canadians in vulnerable situations should be allocated.
It may be of interest to the hon. member that current estimates suggest that the cost of providing a benefit equiva-

February 16, 1978

lent to the income-tested spouse's allowance for all persons in the 60 to 64 age group, as he suggested, would be approximately $635 million in the first year alone. This would be in addition to the cost of the current spouse's allowance benefit, and would be five times the present expenditures on this allowance.
The department advises me that the spouse's allowance was introduced to cover the situation of married couples with little or no other income who were trying to get by on the single pension. It was considered appropriate to use the spouse's allowance for cases like this, because the married couple already had a connection with the old age security program through the one spouse who had reached retirement age.
It is recognized that many other people in the age range 60 to 65 have need for income assistance also. However, it was considered that these needs would be met through another program, the Canada Assistance Plan, under which the government of Canada shares in the cost of income support granted to people in need under the general assistance program of each province.

Of course, when these people reach age 65, they too normally become eligible for the old age security program.
Possibilities for improving income support programs are under review by the federal and provincial governments. The government of Canada is also studying possibilities for providing some form of income supplementation to Canadians who are working at inadequate levels of income. Program changes along these lines may lead eventually to improvements in the income security system for Canadians in the 60 to 64 age range, as well as for other Canadians in vulnerable circumstances. In the meantime, the existing provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan will continue to operate.
In other words, it is our intent to meet the income needs of people under one program or the other, hopefully as effectively as possible.
